6.title: Press On to Maturity: The Anchor of the Soul
6.overview:
Chapter 6 holds both the most debated and the most encouraging passages in the letter. It begins with a call to maturity: build on the foundations, do not keep relaying them. Then comes the severest warning (vv. 4–8): those who have seen the full light of the gospel and then deliberately turn away cannot be restored to repentance. Its pastoral aim is to shock the drifting into seeing what is at stake.

At once the writer turns: “in your case, beloved, we feel sure of better things” (v. 9). He grounds his confidence in God’s faithfulness, who will not forget their love. And the chapter ends with hope as an anchor for the soul, lodged behind the curtain where Jesus has gone ahead as forerunner. Everything is secure because the Priest is already inside.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Hardest Warning, and the Confidence After It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Let us move beyond the elementary teaching about Christ and go on to maturity, not laying again the foundation of repentance, faith, washings, laying on of hands, resurrection and judgment. It is impossible to restore to repentance those who have been enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift, shared in the Holy Spirit and tasted the goodness of God’s word, and then fallen away, because they are crucifying the Son of God again. Land that drinks the rain and bears a crop is blessed; land that bears thorns is near to being cursed. But we are confident of better things in your case, beloved, because God will not forget your love. Keep your earnestness to the end, imitating those who through faith and patience inherit the promises.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Passage Set Out Honestly

Sincere Christians read verses 4–6 differently. The list describes what was received and seen, not what saves; and five verses later the writer calls his readers beloved and speaks of things that belong to salvation.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Two fields drink the same rain; the crop shows the soil.

Now: The warning is not addressed to the anxious. God is not unjust so as to overlook love shown in serving the saints.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let us leave the elementary doctrine of Christ and go on to maturity, not laying again a foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith toward God, and of instruction about washings, the laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment. And this we will do if God permits.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So let us move beyond the elementary teachings about Christ and be taken forward to maturity, not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works and faith in God, instruction about washings, the laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead and eternal judgment. And God permitting, we will do so.

Leave the foundation? The image is a building. You do not abandon a foundation by building on it, but by digging it up every few years to check it is still there. That is what these readers were doing.

Three pairs. Repentance and faith: the two sides of conversion. Washings and laying on of hands: probably the rites of initiation; “washings” is plural, suggesting teaching Jewish converts how Christian baptism differs from the cleansings they knew. Resurrection and judgment: the end.

Laying on of hands. Used to bless, to commission (Acts 6:6; 13:3), and in the apostles’ ministry when the Spirit was given (Acts 8:17). That last belonged to the apostolic foundation; commissioning with prayer continues.

Nothing distinctively Christian. A devout Pharisee could have affirmed every item. These readers had stalled where Judaism and Christianity overlap, never reaching what is peculiar to Christ: his priesthood, sacrifice and finished work. That is why going back looked so easy.

If God permits. Growth in understanding is granted, not just willed.

verseByVerse.quote: For it is impossible, in the case of those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, and have shared in the Holy Spirit, and have tasted the goodness of the word of God and the powers of the age to come,
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, shared in the Holy Spirit, and tasted the goodness of God’s word and the powers of the coming age,

A formidable description. Enlightened: light has fallen on them. Tasted: not a sip; Jesus “tasted” death (2:9). Shared in the Holy Spirit: the word used of sharing in Christ (3:14). They have found God’s word good and seen the future break into the present in miracles (2:4). Whatever this means, it cannot be dismissed by saying these people were never involved at all.

What is missing. Every term describes something received, experienced or seen. None says they were justified, born again, forgiven or loved by God. Five verses later the writer uses that language of his readers, “beloved” and “things that belong to salvation”. Here he does not.

verseByVerse.quote: and then have fallen away, to restore them again to repentance, since they are crucifying once again the Son of God to their own harm and holding him up to contempt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and who then fall away, to be brought back to repentance, because to their own loss they are crucifying the Son of God all over again and subjecting him to public disgrace.

Fallen away. A strong word: to defect. Not stumbling into sin, but deliberately abandoning the living God (3:12).

Crucifying again. Present tense: while they are doing this. Someone in the act of publicly repudiating Christ cannot at the same time be repenting. “Holding him up to contempt” is public: they have gone back and said, before witnesses, that the crucified man deserved it.

Three readings. First, true believers who lose salvation. But the letter says Christ saves to the uttermost and always intercedes (7:25), and on this reading the loss would be permanent, which few who hold it teach. Second, a hypothetical: if this happened, restoration would be impossible, but it does not happen. That fits the theology but reads thinly against the urgency. Third, people who came very close and were never united to Christ: they saw, tasted, shared in the Spirit’s work among them, and finally repudiated it, like those who “went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19). The third best fits the letter’s own wording and the illustration that follows.

Not addressed to the anxious. A person terrified that this describes him shows the very tenderness the passage says is absent. You cannot grieve over having become unable to repent. The people in view are not agonising; they have walked out.

What about backsliders? This does not describe the believer who has fallen into sin for a season. Peter denied Christ three times, and Jesus had prayed for him: “when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32). The warning is against final apostasy. Whoever wants to come back may come: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). The church is to restore such a person gently (Galatians 6:1).

On a Tuesday. A man who walked away from church years ago reads this and fears he is beyond hope. His fear shows he is not. He should go to Christ today, and to a pastor tomorrow.
verseByVerse.note: Christians have read this warning in different ways; all agree it is a real warning against turning away from Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: For land that has drunk the rain that often falls on it, and produces a crop useful to those for whose sake it is cultivated, receives a blessing from God. But if it bears thorns and thistles, it is worthless and near to being cursed, and its end is to be burned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Land that drinks the rain often falling on it and produces a crop useful to those who farm it receives God’s blessing. But land that produces thorns and thistles is worthless and close to being cursed. In the end it will be burned.

The same rain. One field, the same sky, the same cultivation, and the ground genuinely drinks it in, matching the tasting of vv. 4–5.

Two outcomes. A useful crop, or thorns. Rain absorbed does not determine what grows. What distinguishes the fields is the soil, and the only way to tell is to wait and see what comes up.

Thorns and thistles. The words of the curse in Eden (Genesis 3:18).

Near. The writer does not say the field is cursed, but “near to being cursed”. Near is not yet. While a field is only near, there is time for something else to grow, and this whole letter is written to make that happen.

How to tell. Not by how much was tasted, but by what is growing now.

verseByVerse.quote: Though we speak in this way, yet in your case, beloved, we feel sure of better things—things that belong to salvation. For God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love that you have shown for his name in serving the saints, as you still do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even though we speak like this, dear friends, we are confident of better things in your case, things that come with salvation. God is not unjust; he will not forget your work and the love you have shown him as you have helped his people and continue to help them.

Beloved. The only time he uses the word, right after his severest paragraph.

Things that belong to salvation. The very category missing from vv. 4–5. He knows the difference.

The evidence is the crop. They may be dull of hearing, but they are still serving fellow believers, “as you still do”. That is fruit.

Not owed, but not forgotten. Their service has not earned salvation. But a God who produced such fruit and then discarded the field would be unjust towards his own work.

On a Tuesday. The meals taken to a sick home, years of faithful kindness to awkward people, the unnoticed hours: God is not unjust so as to overlook them. He may be the only one who has not.

verseByVerse.quote: And we desire each one of you to show the same earnestness to have the full assurance of hope until the end, so that you may not be sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We want each of you to show this same diligence to the very end, so that what you hope for may be fully realised. We do not want you to become lazy, but to imitate those who through faith and patience inherit what has been promised.

Each one. Confidence in the congregation must not become a blanket over someone quietly slipping.

The same earnestness. Apply to your hope the diligence you already give your neighbours.

Full assurance. Something to be pursued, not just a feeling that comes or goes.

Sluggish. Nōthros again (5:11): sluggish ears and sluggish lives are one condition.

Faith and patience. Faith takes God at his word; patience keeps taking him at it for years. That is what had run out. Chapter 11 will supply the examples.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–20 — Two Unchangeable Things, and an Anchor Behind the Curtain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When God made his promise to Abraham, he swore by himself, since there was no one greater, and Abraham, after waiting patiently, received what was promised. People swear by something greater, and an oath settles a dispute. So God, wanting to show the heirs of the promise how unchangeable his purpose is, confirmed it with an oath. By these two unchangeable things, in which God cannot lie, we who have fled to him for refuge are strongly encouraged to hold fast to our hope. It is a sure anchor for the soul, entering behind the curtain where Jesus has gone ahead of us.
verseByVerse.theology:
An Anchor That Goes Upward

God confirmed his promise with an oath so that we might have strong encouragement. Our hope is anchored behind the curtain, where Jesus has gone ahead of us as forerunner.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Abraham waited twenty-five years for Isaac, not always steadily, and obtained the promise.

Now: We are those who have fled for refuge. The storm and the anchorage are in different places.

verseByVerse.quote: For when God made a promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself, saying, “Surely I will bless you and multiply you.” And thus Abraham, having patiently waited, obtained the promise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God made his promise to Abraham, since there was no one greater to swear by, he swore by himself, saying, “I will surely bless you and give you many descendants.” And so, after waiting patiently, Abraham received what was promised.

The occasion. Genesis 22, just after Abraham raised the knife over Isaac.

He swore by himself. An oath invokes something greater as surety. God has nothing greater, so the guarantee is his own existence. For the promise to fail, he would have to stop being God.

Patiently waited. Abraham was seventy-five when promised, a hundred when Isaac was born: twenty-five years, twice trying to arrange it himself, once laughing at God. The waiting was not serene. Hebrews still calls it patience.

A comfort. What the New Testament commends in Abraham is not that he never wobbled, but that he was still there at the end.

Obtained, yet not yet. He received Isaac, but not the city or the blessing to all nations (11:13). Kept, and not yet finished: the readers’ position too.

verseByVerse.quote: For people swear by something greater than themselves, and in all their disputes an oath is final for confirmation. So when God desired to show more convincingly to the heirs of the promise the unchangeable character of his purpose, he guaranteed it with an oath, so that by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
People swear by someone greater than themselves, and an oath confirms what is said and ends all argument. Because God wanted to make the unchanging nature of his purpose very clear to the heirs of the promise, he confirmed it with an oath. He did this so that, by two unchangeable things in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us may be greatly encouraged.

Why oaths exist. People are not reliably truthful, so societies invent a way to end argument.

To convince us. God’s bare word is already perfectly reliable; an oath adds nothing to him and everything to our confidence. He swore it for our sake.

The heirs. An oath sworn to one old man on a mountain, for everyone who would inherit it, including you.

Two unchangeable things. His promise and his oath. And “impossible” echoes v. 4. The letter’s two impossibilities face each other: it is impossible to restore an apostate, and impossible for God to lie. Build on the second.

Fled for refuge. The cities of refuge (Numbers 35): a man pursued by the avenger ran for his life to the walled town, safe inside, dead outside. Not a seeker weighing options, but a man running to the only place that will hold him.

On a Tuesday. When your hope is shaken, do not look first at your feelings. Look at God’s promise and oath. He cannot lie. Hold on.

verseByVerse.quote: We have this as a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul, a hope that enters into the inner place behind the curtain, where Jesus has gone as a forerunner on our behalf, having become a high priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have this hope as a firm and secure anchor for the soul. It enters the inner sanctuary behind the curtain, where Jesus, who went before us, has entered on our behalf. He has become a high priest forever, in the order of Melchizedek.

Sure and steadfast. An anchor fails by breaking or by dragging. This one does neither.

An anchor that goes up. Anchors go down. This one goes up and in, behind the curtain of the Most Holy Place. The cable runs out of this world and is fixed in God’s sanctuary, not in circumstances or in our own steadiness.

The storm and the anchorage are in different places. A ship in a gale is held by ground it cannot see. The state of the sea has no bearing on the holding.

Forerunner. Prodromos: a scout sent ahead so that others can follow. The old high priest went in alone, came out, and no one followed. This one went in and stayed, and the rope is attached to us.

For worship. Your hope is not in your grip on Christ, but in Christ’s place before the Father. Rest there.
verseByVerse.note: The high priest passed behind the curtain into the Most Holy Place once a year, on the Day of Atonement.

7.title: The Order of Melchizedek: A Priest Forever
7.overview:
Chapter 7 is the theological centre of Hebrews. From two brief Old Testament references, Genesis 14:17–20 and Psalm 110:4, the writer argues for the supremacy and finality of Jesus’ priesthood over the whole Levitical system.

Melchizedek was king of righteousness and king of peace, priest of God Most High, king and priest in one. Genesis gives him no genealogy, birth or death, and that silence makes him a picture of the eternal Son. Abraham gave him a tenth and received his blessing, so Melchizedek was greater than Abraham and, in Abraham, greater than Levi. If the Levitical priesthood had brought perfection, why promise another? Jesus is a priest “by the power of an indestructible life”, guarantor of a better covenant, able to save to the uttermost because he always lives to intercede.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Melchizedek, and What Abraham Did
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, met Abraham after the battle, blessed him and received a tenth of the spoils. His name means king of righteousness; Salem means peace. Without recorded father, mother or genealogy, beginning or end, he resembles the Son of God and remains a priest. Abraham the patriarch paid him tithes and was blessed by him, and the lesser is blessed by the greater. Even Levi, still in Abraham’s body, paid tithes through him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Reading the Silence of Scripture

Genesis gives Melchizedek no genealogy, and the writer reads the silence as a portrait of a priesthood that does not rest on descent. Abraham tithed to him and was blessed by him — the lesser by the greater.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Levi, still in Abraham's loins, paid tithes to Melchizedek.

Now: Righteousness comes first, then peace; there is no peace with God that bypasses righteousness.

verseByVerse.quote: For this Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of the Most High God, met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him, and to him Abraham apportioned a tenth part of everything. He is first, by translation of his name, king of righteousness, and then he is also king of Salem, that is, king of peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, met Abraham returning from defeating the kings and blessed him, and Abraham gave him a tenth of everything. His name means “king of righteousness”; and “king of Salem” means “king of peace”.

Genesis 14. Returning from rescuing Lot, Abraham meets a stranger who brings bread and wine, blesses him, receives a tenth, and vanishes from the story.

Priest of the Most High. Centuries before Sinai or Levi, a Canaanite king is already a priest of the true God, and Abraham recognises it.

The names. Melek (king) and tsedeq (righteousness); Salem from shalem, related to shalom, peace. Salem is probably the old name of Jerusalem (Psalm 76:2).

First righteousness, then peace. The order is the shape of the gospel. There is no peace with God that bypasses righteousness. That is why the cross was necessary.

For worship. Christ is our King of righteousness who gives us his righteousness, and so our King of peace.

verseByVerse.quote: He is without father or mother or genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but resembling the Son of God he continues a priest forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without father or mother, without genealogy, without beginning of days or end of life, resembling the Son of God, he remains a priest forever.

Was he an angel or Christ himself? Some have read it so. But the last clause says he resembles the Son of God, and a thing does not resemble itself. He was a real man.

Reading the silence. Genesis is full of genealogies, births and deaths. Melchizedek walks in with none. For a priest that is extraordinary: Levitical priesthood depended entirely on documented descent; after the exile, men without records were excluded (Ezra 2:61–62). The writer takes the silence as deliberate: Scripture sketches a priesthood not based on descent and not ended by death.

The direction. Not that Christ is like Melchizedek, but that Melchizedek was made to resemble the Son. The reality came first; the man in Genesis is the sketch.

Forever. True of Melchizedek only in that the text never records him stopping. True of Christ absolutely.
verseByVerse.note: Genesis records no parents, birth or death for Melchizedek. The writer draws out the meaning of that silence, not a claim that Melchizedek had no parents.

verseByVerse.quote: See how great this man was to whom Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth of the spoils! And those descendants of Levi who receive the priestly office have a commandment in the law to take tithes from the people, that is, from their brothers, though these also are descended from Abraham. But this man who does not have his descent from them received tithes from Abraham and blessed him who had the promises. It is beyond dispute that the inferior is blessed by the superior.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consider how great he was: even the patriarch Abraham gave him a tenth of the spoils. The descendants of Levi who become priests are commanded by the law to collect tithes from the people, their own relatives, though they too descend from Abraham. But Melchizedek, who was not descended from Levi, collected a tenth from Abraham and blessed the one who had the promises. And without doubt the lesser is blessed by the greater.

The patriarch. The highest name a Jewish reader had. Whatever is proved, is proved against that standard.

Given, not levied. Levites collected from relatives of equal standing, by written command. Melchizedek had no legal warrant, and the payer was Abraham himself.

Blessing runs downhill. Father to son, priest to people. Nobody blesses upward. Abraham, holder of the promises, took the lower place twice in one meeting.

Must Christians tithe? Some say yes, at least as a minimum: Abraham tithed before the law (and Jacob, Genesis 28:22), and Jesus told the Pharisees not to neglect it (Matthew 23:23). But Abraham’s tenth was a single gift from spoils, not a rule; the law’s tithes belonged to the Levitical system this chapter says has changed (v. 12); and Jesus spoke to men still under that law. The New Testament never commands tithing. It teaches giving that is regular, proportionate and glad (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 9:7). The tithe is not binding, but it is a good place for many to begin, and those under the better covenant will hardly want to give less than those under the old.

verseByVerse.quote: In the one case tithes are received by mortal men, but in the other case, by one of whom it is testified that he lives. One might even say that Levi himself, who receives tithes, paid tithes through Abraham, for he was still in the loins of his ancestor when Melchizedek met him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In one case, the tithe is collected by men who die; in the other, by him who is declared to be living. One might even say that Levi, who collects the tenth, paid the tenth through Abraham, because when Melchizedek met Abraham, Levi was still in his ancestor’s body.

Mortal men. The Levitical priesthood was a relay: Aaron served and died, Eleazar took the robes, and so on for fourteen centuries. It was designed around death.

“Testified that he lives”. The claim rests on what the text records and leaves out.

“One might even say”. Offered as a way of seeing, not a knock-down proof. Levi was Abraham’s great-grandson, yet in Hebrew thinking a descendant is present in his ancestor.

Representative solidarity. That principle is the logic of salvation itself: one man’s sin involved the race; one man’s obedience makes many righteous (Romans 5:12–19).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–28 — A Priest Forever, and the Change That Follows
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If perfection had come through the Levitical priesthood, why promise another of a different order? A change of priesthood means a change of law. Jesus came from Judah, a tribe with no priests, and he is a priest not by descent but by the power of an indestructible life. The old command is set aside as weak; a better hope lets us draw near to God. God swore an oath to this priesthood, making Jesus guarantor of a better covenant. The old priests were many because they died; he lives forever, so he saves completely those who come to God through him, always interceding. Holy and exalted, he offered himself once for all.
verseByVerse.theology:
Change the Priesthood and the Law Must Follow

The law rested on the Levitical priesthood, and God has replaced that priesthood by oath with a priest who holds office by the power of an indestructible life.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The former priests were many, because death stopped each one.

Now: He is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to intercede for them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if perfection had been attainable through the Levitical priesthood (for under it the people received the law), what further need would there have been for another priest to arise after the order of Melchizedek, rather than one named after the order of Aaron? For when there is a change in the priesthood, there is necessarily a change in the law as well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If perfection could have been reached through the Levitical priesthood, on which the law given to the people was based, why was there still a need for another priest to come, in the order of Melchizedek, not of Aaron? When the priesthood changes, the law must change too.

You do not replace what works. Psalm 110 was written centuries into the Levitical system, announcing a new priest. The promise itself shows the old arrangement was not final.

Perfection. Completion, reaching the goal. Not whether it was good, but whether it could finish anything.

Priesthood and law together. The law was given through the priestly system and depends on it. Change the foundation, and the superstructure cannot stand as it did.

Are the Ten Commandments abolished? No. The law that changes is the law bound up with the priesthood: sacrifices, temple, purity rules, calendar. Reformed Christians distinguish the ceremonial law (fulfilled in Christ), the civil law (given to Israel as a nation) and the moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, which still shows believers how to love God and neighbour (Matthew 5:17–19; Romans 13:8–10). Some prefer to say the whole Mosaic law has given way to the law of Christ, but agree that its moral demands return in the New Testament, written on the heart (8:10). What changes is not God’s standard but the way to him.

verseByVerse.quote: For the one of whom these things are spoken belonged to another tribe, from which no one has ever served at the altar. For it is evident that our Lord was descended from Judah, and in connection with that tribe Moses said nothing about priests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He of whom these things are said belonged to a different tribe, and no one from that tribe has ever served at the altar. It is clear that our Lord descended from Judah, and Moses said nothing about priests from that tribe.

The obstacle. In fourteen hundred years no one from Judah ever served at the altar.

Evident. Jesus’ descent from Judah and David was common knowledge.

The collision. The Messiah must be from Judah (the promise); a priest must be from Levi (the law); Psalm 110 says the Messiah will be a priest.

Another silence. Moses said nothing about priests from Judah, because this priesthood was never going to run through the law.

The objection conceded. Jesus had no claim to Levitical priesthood, and never made one. He holds a different, older office established by oath.

verseByVerse.quote: This becomes even more evident when another priest arises in the likeness of Melchizedek, who has become a priest, not on the basis of a legal requirement concerning bodily descent, but by the power of an indestructible life. For it is witnessed of him, “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is even clearer since another priest like Melchizedek appears, one who has become a priest not by a rule about ancestry but by the power of an indestructible life. For it is declared, “You are a priest forever, in the order of Melchizedek.”

Another of a different kind. Not a successor, but a different kind of priest.

Pedigree or life. Old priests qualified by their birth certificate: a godly Israelite from the wrong tribe could not serve; an indifferent one from the right family could. Christ qualifies by “the power of an indestructible life”, a life that cannot be dissolved, with the resurrection behind the phrase.

Records or an empty tomb. One priesthood rests on records that can be lost (Ezra 2:61–62); the other on an empty tomb.

Forever. A priest forever needs no successor, takes no holiday and cannot be bettered.

verseByVerse.quote: For on the one hand, a former commandment is set aside because of its weakness and uselessness (for the law made nothing perfect); but on the other hand, a better hope is introduced, through which we draw near to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The former regulation is set aside because it was weak and useless (for the law made nothing perfect), and a better hope is introduced, by which we draw near to God.

Weak and useless? Strong words about God’s own law, and they must be read exactly. Not that the law was evil or a mistake. It did what it was given to do: exposed sin, ordered a nation, pointed forward. It was useless for making anyone perfect, which it never claimed to do. A thermometer is useless for heating a room, and the fault is not in the thermometer.

Nothing perfect. In fourteen centuries the whole system brought nothing to completion.

Better. The letter’s signature word, used thirteen times.

Draw near. The goal of it all. The old system managed distance with curtains and courts; the new removes it (4:16; 10:22).

On a Tuesday. If you still try to approach God through your own record, stop. The better hope is not a better you, but a better priest. Draw near through him.

verseByVerse.quote: And it was not without an oath. For those who formerly became priests were made such without an oath, but this one was made a priest with an oath by the one who said to him: “The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind, ’You are a priest forever.’” This makes Jesus the guarantor of a better covenant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And it was not without an oath. Others became priests without any oath, but he became a priest with an oath when God said to him, “The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind: ‘You are a priest forever.’” Because of this oath, Jesus has become the guarantor of a better covenant.

No oath for Levi. Exodus and Leviticus are full of instructions about priests, and God never swears to them. He legislated; he did not guarantee.

Sworn and irreversible. A command can be amended by a later command, and the Levitical system was. An arrangement established by God’s oath, who cannot lie (6:18), cannot.

Guarantor. Engyos, used only here in the New Testament: a surety who stands behind an obligation with his own person. If the debtor fails, the guarantor pays. Covenants fail because one side fails, as the first one did. Jesus stands behind the new covenant with himself, so it cannot fail on our side.

verseByVerse.quote: The former priests were many in number, because they were prevented by death from continuing in office, but he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever. Consequently, he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There were many former priests, since death prevented them from continuing in office. But because Jesus lives forever, he has a permanent priesthood. So he is able to save completely those who come to God through him, because he always lives to intercede for them.

Eighty funerals. Tradition counted about eighty high priests from Aaron to the temple’s fall. Whatever confidence you had in your priest died with him.

Permanent. Not transferable, never handed on.

To the uttermost. Completely, or forever; both are true. Nothing in a person is beyond its reach, and no length of time outlasts it.

Those who draw near. The only qualification named. Not those who understand or have never failed: those who come.

Always interceding. What is Christ doing now? Praying for his people, without pause.

Do Christians need human priests? No. Christ holds his priesthood permanently and offered himself “once for all” (v. 27). Roman Catholic teaching holds that in the Mass the one sacrifice of Christ is made present and offered by the priest. But this letter says Christ has no need to offer sacrifice daily, because he did it once (10:11–14). Every believer draws near to God through him (4:16; 10:19–22), and the whole church is “a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9). Pastors are shepherds and teachers, not priests.

On a Tuesday. At three in the morning, too tired or ashamed to pray, remember: someone at the Father’s right hand is praying for you and has not stopped.

verseByVerse.quote: For it was indeed fitting that we should have such a high priest, holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners, and exalted above the heavens. He has no need, like those high priests, to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins and then for those of the people, since he did this once for all when he offered up himself. For the law appoints men in their weakness as high priests, but the word of the oath, which came later than the law, appoints a Son who has been made perfect forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Such a high priest truly meets our need: holy, blameless, pure, set apart from sinners, exalted above the heavens. Unlike the other high priests, he does not need to offer sacrifices day after day, first for his own sins and then for the people’s. He sacrificed for their sins once for all when he offered himself. The law appoints weak men as high priests, but the oath, which came after the law, appointed the Son, who has been made perfect forever.

Fitting. As in 2:10: it suited God’s character to provide him.

Five descriptions. Holy: devout, wholly given to God. Innocent: without malice. Unstained: undefiled. Separated from sinners: not aloof (he was the friend of sinners), but morally distinct, and now exalted.

Daily, and first for himself. The old priests’ two problems: it never stopped, and they had to deal with their own sin first.

Once for all. Ephapax: never to be repeated (chapters 9–10).

He offered himself. Every other priest brought an animal. This one brought himself. Priest and sacrifice in one person, which no religion had imagined.

Weak men and a Son. A temporary command, and a later oath. Psalm 110 came after Sinai, and God does not swear to what he means to revise.

For worship. Your high priest is holy, and he is for you. Stop and thank him.

8.title: A Better Covenant: Written on the Heart
8.overview:
Chapter 8 caps the argument about priesthood: a better Priest ministers in a better sanctuary under a better covenant. The “main point” (v. 1) is that our high priest is seated at God’s right hand in heaven, serving in the true tent. The earthly tabernacle Moses built was a copy and shadow of the heavenly reality (Exodus 25:40).

The better covenant is then proved by the longest Old Testament quotation in the New: Jeremiah 31:31–34. Written while the temple stood, it promised a new covenant unlike Sinai: law written on the heart, everyone knowing God, and “I will remember their sins no more”. By calling it “new”, God made the old obsolete, and “what is growing old is ready to vanish away”. There is nothing to go back to.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — A Minister in the True Tent
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Here is the main point: we have a high priest seated at the right hand of God’s throne in heaven, serving in the true tent set up by the Lord, not by man. Every high priest must have something to offer. On earth he would not even be a priest, since there are priests under the law, who serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly sanctuary, built to the pattern shown to Moses on the mountain. But Christ’s ministry is far better, as the covenant he mediates is better, founded on better promises.
verseByVerse.theology:
Copy, Shadow, and the Pattern on the Mountain

The earthly tent was a copy of what Moses was shown. Christ ministers in the true tent, and the covenant he mediates is better because it rests on better promises.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Readers grieving the loss of the temple had not been shut out of the sanctuary.

Now: They had been let into the one the sanctuary pictured, where their high priest is seated.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the point in what we are saying is this: we have such a high priest, one who is seated at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven, a minister in the holy places, in the true tent that the Lord set up, not man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The main point is this: we have such a high priest, who sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven, and who serves in the sanctuary, the true tabernacle set up by the Lord, not by a human being.

The point. The chief thing, the sum of the account. A kindness in a long argument.

We have. Not “there is”, but “we have”: present possession, for a frightened congregation.

Seated. No tabernacle priest sat; the work never ended. And at the right hand: sharing the throne’s authority (Psalm 110:1).

Minister. Leitourgos, from which “liturgy” comes: public priestly service for others.

The true tent. Not genuine as against fake; the tabernacle was not a fraud. True as original against copy.

For those grieving the temple. You have not been shut out of the sanctuary. You have been let into the one it pictured, and a man of your own race sits there.

verseByVerse.quote: For every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices; thus it is necessary for this priest also to have something to offer. Now if he were on earth, he would not be a priest at all, since there are priests who offer gifts according to the law. They serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things. For when Moses was about to erect the tent, he was instructed by God, saying, “See that you make everything according to the pattern that was shown you on the mountain.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices, so this one also had to have something to offer. If he were on earth, he would not be a priest, since there are already priests who offer the gifts the law prescribes. They serve at a sanctuary that is a copy and shadow of what is in heaven. That is why Moses was warned, when he was about to build the tabernacle: “See to it that you make everything according to the pattern shown you on the mountain.”

Something to offer. A priest without an offering is a contradiction. The answer was given at 7:27, himself, and is explained in chapters 9–10.

Not a priest on earth. The writer concedes it completely: under the earthly arrangement Jesus has no standing.

Copy and shadow. A copy is a model of something real. A shadow has the shape and none of the substance, and proves the body exists. Neither means false. But nobody prefers the shadow once the person walks in.

The pattern. Exodus 25:40. God showed Moses something and told him to reproduce it. By its own founding charter, the tabernacle was a copy. This is not a Greek idea imposed on Scripture; it is what God said.

Backwards. The readers thought they were leaving the real thing for something less tangible. It was the reverse.

verseByVerse.quote: But as it is, Christ has obtained a ministry that is as much more excellent than the old as the covenant he mediates is better, since it is enacted on better promises.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Jesus has received a ministry far better than theirs, just as the covenant he mediates is better, since it is founded on better promises.

Measured, not asserted. The minister’s superiority matches the covenant’s, as at 1:4.

Mediator. Moses stood between a holy God and a terrified people (Exodus 20:19), carried the terms down and the answer up, and the covenant failed anyway. This mediator is also the guarantor (7:22) and the sacrifice (7:27). He does not only convey the covenant; he pays for it.

Better promises. Not easier rules or a lower standard, but what God undertakes to do. The old covenant said, “Do this and live.” The new says, “I will put my laws in their hearts; I will be merciful; I will remember their sins no more.” The verbs have changed hands.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — The New Covenant Promised by Jeremiah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If the first covenant had been without fault, there would have been no need for a second. But God found fault with the people and promised through Jeremiah a new covenant, unlike the one at Sinai which they broke. He would write his laws on their hearts, be their God, and all would know him, from the least to the greatest, for he would forgive their sins and remember them no more. By calling it new, he made the first obsolete, and what is obsolete will soon disappear.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Verbs Have Changed Hands

In Jeremiah's promise God says “I will”: the law written on the heart, knowledge of God for all, and sins remembered no more.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: God found fault with the people, not with the covenant.

Now: God does not forget; he has resolved never to act toward his people on the basis of their sins.

verseByVerse.quote: For if that first covenant had been faultless, there would have been no occasion to look for a second. For he finds fault with them when he says: “Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord, when I will establish a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt. For they did not continue in my covenant, and so I showed no concern for them, declares the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the first covenant had been faultless, there would have been no need for a second. But God found fault with the people and said: “The days are coming, declares the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the people of Israel and Judah. It will not be like the covenant I made with their ancestors when I took them by the hand to lead them out of Egypt, because they did not remain faithful to my covenant, and I turned away from them.”

A promised replacement. As with the priesthood (7:11), God does not announce a new covenant while the old is doing everything needed.

Fault with them. Not with it. The law is holy, righteous and good; what it could not do was weakened by the flesh (Romans 7:12; 8:3). A perfect law given to imperfect people cannot produce righteousness.

Jeremiah 31:31–34. All four verses in full: the Old Testament itself announced the old arrangement’s end.

Who is it for? The promise is to Israel and Judah. Dispensational Christians hold it will be fulfilled to national Israel in the future, the church sharing some blessings. But Hebrews quotes it to explain what Christ has already done for its readers: he mediates it now (v. 6; 9:15), the Spirit bears witness to it now (10:15–17), and believers have come to “Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant” (12:24). The more likely reading is that it is fulfilled in Christ and his people, Jew and Gentile together, its fullness awaiting his return (Romans 11:26–27).

Hope at the point of ruin. Jeremiah spoke this as exile closed in.

By the hand. God describes the exodus as leading a child.
verseByVerse.note: The longest Old Testament quotation in the New Testament runs from v. 8 to v. 12.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws into their minds, and write them on their hearts, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And they shall not teach, each one his neighbor and each one his brother, saying, ’Know the Lord,’ for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the covenant I will make with Israel after that time, declares the Lord: I will put my laws in their minds and write them on their hearts. I will be their God, and they will be my people. No longer will they teach their neighbour or say to one another, “Know the Lord”, because they will all know me, from the least to the greatest.

Count the “I will”s. God undertakes it.

Same law, new place. God does not promise a different or easier law. It moves from stone to heart. The problem was never the standard but that it was outside people who did not want it. The remedy is a new heart that wants what the law commands.

Do the Ten Commandments still bind? Yes, as the moral law God writes on the heart, though not as terms by which we earn life. What becomes obsolete (v. 13) is the Mosaic administration: priesthood, sacrifices, temple, and Israel’s civil law. Some speak instead of the law of Christ replacing the law of Moses; the practical result is close, since nine of the ten commandments reappear in the New Testament. The fourth looks different, because its Sabbath rest is fulfilled in Christ (4:9–10; Colossians 2:16–17).

The covenant formula. “I will be their God, and they shall be my people”: said to Abraham, at Sinai, by the prophets, and at last in the new creation (Revelation 21:3).

No second-hand members. Not that teaching stops; this letter is a sermon. Under the old arrangement you could be born into the nation and never know God, like the wilderness generation. Under the new, everyone in it knows him, from least to greatest. No inner circle.

On a Tuesday. If you find yourself wanting to obey God, not just feeling you should, that desire is the new covenant at work in you. Thank him.

verseByVerse.quote: For I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I will forgive their wickedness and will remember their sins no more.

For. The foundation of everything else. Law on the heart, knowing God: none of it can happen while sin is unresolved.

What “remember no more” does not mean. Not that God forgets. An all-knowing God does not misplace information, and a God who could would be smaller, not kinder.

What it does mean. In Hebrew, to remember is to act on. God remembered Noah and acted for him (Genesis 8:1); the thief asked to be remembered (Luke 23:42). Not remembering sins is a settled resolve never to act towards the sinner on the basis of them. That is stronger than forgetting: a forgetful God might be reminded.

Reversing the old. The old sacrifices were an annual reminder of sins (10:3). The readers were being drawn back to a calendar that existed to bring their sins to mind, and away from a covenant in which God has promised never to raise them.

On a Tuesday. When an old sin comes back to accuse you, answer with God’s promise: “He remembers it no more.” If he will not bring it up, you need not either.

verseByVerse.quote: In speaking of a new covenant, he makes the first one obsolete. And what is becoming obsolete and growing old is ready to vanish away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By calling this covenant “new”, he has made the first one obsolete, and what is obsolete and ageing will soon disappear.

One adjective. You cannot call something new without making something else old. Jeremiah pronounced the first covenant obsolete six centuries ahead.

Growing old. A word for clothing wearing out and bodies ageing.

Near to vanishing. When this was written, the temple was standing and the sacrifices were offered daily; the writer uses the present tense. Probably within a few years, in AD 70, the temple was destroyed, and the sacrifices have never resumed.

What they were looking at. A busy temple, smoke rising every morning, looking permanent. The writer tells them: an institution in its last days, kept going by habit, while the reality it pictured sits at God’s right hand. Going back would be stepping onto a floor about to give way.

For worship. Everything else ages. The new covenant, sealed in Christ’s blood, never will.
