9.title: The Blood of Christ: Once for All Into the Holy Place
9.overview:
Chapter 9 is the beating heart of Hebrews’ theology of atonement. The writer moves from the sanctuary to the sacrifice, showing how the structure of the Mosaic tabernacle was itself a theological sermon about access to God — restricted access, mediated access, temporary access — and how Jesus has opened what the tabernacle could only describe.

The tabernacle’s two-room structure is unpacked with theological precision: the outer tent (the Holy Place), entered by priests daily; the inner tent (the Most Holy Place), entered only by the high priest, only once a year, only with blood. The Spirit was teaching through this architecture: the way into the presence of God was not yet fully open. The wall between the Holy Place and the Most Holy Place was a living parable of the barrier between sinful humanity and the holy God. It required a perfect sacrifice to tear that wall down — not in cedar and gold but in flesh and blood.

When Christ appeared as high priest, he entered not through curtains of linen and animal skins but through “the greater and more perfect tent not made with hands” (v. 11) — the heavenly sanctuary, the very presence of God. And he entered not with the blood of goats and calves but with his own blood. Once. That word — “once” (ephapax) — rings like a bell through the chapter. Once, finally, permanently, securing an eternal redemption. The chapter closes with the most comprehensive statement of Christ’s atoning purpose in the letter: “to bear the sins of many.” He carried what we could not carry. He appeared before God bearing the full weight of our guilt. And he will appear a second time — not to deal with sin again, because that was done — but to bring salvation to its final consummation for all who eagerly wait for him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Closed Door, and the Blood That Opened It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The first covenant had regulations for worship and an earthly sanctuary (v.1): an outer tent with lampstand, table and bread of the Presence, called the Holy Place (v.2), and behind a second curtain the Most Holy Place (v.3), holding the golden altar of incense and the ark, containing the manna, Aaron’s budded staff and the tablets (v.4), overshadowed by the cherubim above the mercy seat (v.5).

Priests entered the first section regularly (v.6), but the second only the high priest, once a year, never without blood, offered first for himself and then for the unintentional sins of the people (v.7). By this the Holy Spirit indicates that the way in was not yet opened while the first section stood (v.8) — a parable for the present age, in which gifts and sacrifices cannot perfect the worshipper’s conscience (v.9), dealing only with food, drink and washings until the time of reformation (v.10).

But Christ appeared as high priest of the good things that have come, through a greater tent not of this creation (v.11), entering once for all by his own blood and securing an eternal redemption (v.12). If the blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer purify the flesh (v.13), how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish, purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God (v.14).
verseByVerse.theology:
Architecture That Preached

By the tabernacle's design the Holy Spirit was saying not yet: one man, one day a year, never without blood. Its sacrifices could not perfect the conscience; the blood of Christ does.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The ark held manna, Aaron's staff and the tablets, with the mercy seat over them.

Now: A cleansed conscience is set free from dead works to serve the living God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now even the first covenant had regulations for worship and an earthly place of holiness. For a tent was prepared, the first section, in which were the lampstand and the table and the bread of the Presence. It is called the Holy Place. Behind the second curtain was a second section called the Most Holy Place, having the golden altar of incense and the ark of the covenant covered on all sides with gold, in which was a golden urn holding the manna, and Aaron’s staff that budded, and the tablets of the covenant. Above it were the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat. Of these things we cannot now speak in detail.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The writer takes his readers on a tour of the tabernacle, and the tour has a purpose: he wants them to see the building he is about to declare obsolete, and to feel how good it was.

“Even the first covenant had regulations for worship and an earthly place of holiness.” Both terms are respectful. It was real worship, divinely regulated, in a genuinely holy place. The adjective “earthly” is the only hint of limitation, and it is doing all the work.

“A tent was prepared, the first section… the lampstand and the table and the bread of the Presence.” The Holy Place: a golden seven-branched lamp, burning perpetually because there were no windows, and a table with twelve loaves renewed every Sabbath, one for each tribe, set out before God.

“Behind the second curtain was a second section called the Most Holy Place.” And the mention of a curtain is not incidental. There were two, and they were the point of the architecture: barriers, in a building designed to teach people how far away they were.

Inside were the ark and its contents, and the three objects are a small sermon in themselves. “A golden urn holding the manna” — bread from heaven for people who grumbled about the food. “Aaron’s staff that budded” — a dead stick that flowered overnight to settle a rebellion against the priesthood (Num 17). “And the tablets of the covenant” — the law they had broken before Moses got down the mountain.

Two details have puzzled readers. First, 1 Kings 8:9 says that in Solomon’s day there was nothing in the ark except the two tablets of stone. But the writer is describing the tabernacle of Moses’ day, when the urn of manna and Aaron’s staff were kept with the ark before the testimony (Exod 16:34; Num 17:10); by Solomon’s time, centuries later, only the tablets remained. Second, the writer says the Most Holy Place had the golden altar of incense, though the altar stood just outside the curtain (Exod 30:6). It stood in front of the mercy seat, its incense was carried inside on the Day of Atonement (Lev 16:12–13), and 1 Kings 6:22 likewise speaks of the whole altar that belonged to the inner sanctuary. It belonged to the worship of the inner room, and neither detail touches the writer’s point.

Three memorials of Israel’s failure, kept in a gold box in the holiest room in the world. And on top of them, “the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat” — the lid, where blood was sprinkled once a year. The record of the rebellion is inside the box, and the covering where mercy is applied lies directly over it.

“Of these things we cannot now speak in detail.” The preacher pulls himself up, and one senses he would have liked to. He has an argument to make, and it is not about furniture.

verseByVerse.quote: These preparations having thus been made, the priests go regularly into the first section, performing their ritual duties, but into the second only the high priest goes, and he but once a year, and not without taking blood, which he offers for himself and for the unintentional sins of the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the writer moves from the architecture to what actually happened in it, and every detail is chosen to make a single point about access.

“The priests go regularly into the first section, performing their ritual duties.” Note the present tense throughout this passage — the temple was still operating as he wrote. Priests went into the Holy Place daily, trimming the lamps and burning incense. Routine, frequent, ordinary.

“But into the second…” and now come the restrictions, piled one on another.

Only the high priest — one man out of a nation. Once a year — one day out of three hundred and sixty-five. Not without taking blood — and never on his own account. Which he offers for himself, and first — because the man doing the representing was himself part of the problem.

Four limitations in a single sentence, and their combined effect is arithmetic: for some fourteen centuries, access to the presence of God amounted to one man, one day, with a basin of blood, having first dealt with his own sin.

And the last phrase is the sharpest: he offers it “for the unintentional sins of the people.” The Day of Atonement covered sins committed in ignorance and error. For the deliberate, high-handed sin the law made no provision at all (Num 15:30–31).

Sit with what that meant for a thoughtful Israelite. The most solemn day in the calendar, the whole nation fasting, the high priest behind the curtain — and the sins that troubled a man most, the ones he chose with his eyes open, were precisely the ones the ceremony did not reach.

That is the gap this letter exists to fill, and the writer has built it carefully. He is not attacking the old system. He is describing it accurately until his readers feel its shape — and the shape is a closed door.

verseByVerse.quote: By this the Holy Spirit indicates that the way into the holy places is not yet opened as long as the first section is still standing (which is symbolic for the present age). According to this arrangement, gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot perfect the conscience of the worshiper, but deal only with food and drink and various washings, regulations for the body imposed until the time of reformation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“By this the Holy Spirit indicates” — and the phrase repays a stop. The writer is not saying the tabernacle’s design happened to suggest something. He says the Holy Spirit was speaking through the architecture.

The curtains, the restrictions, the single day: these were not merely practical arrangements for a holy God. They were a sermon in cloth and gold, preached silently for centuries.

And the message was: “the way into the holy places is not yet opened as long as the first section is still standing.” The old sanctuary’s chief function was to say not yet. Every priest who walked into the Holy Place and stopped at the second curtain was preaching it.

“(Which is symbolic for the present age.)” The word is parabole — a parable. The tabernacle was an acted parable, and its meaning was still being worked out while the temple stood.

Then the verdict, and it is the heart of the chapter: “gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot perfect the conscience of the worshiper.”

There is the limitation, named exactly. Not that the sacrifices did nothing — they did what they were given to do. What they could not do was reach the conscience. A man could bring his goat, watch it die, see the blood applied, walk home ceremonially clean, and still know perfectly well what he had done.

That is a description anyone can verify from the inside. Religious observance can leave a person outwardly regular and inwardly unrelieved — and the writer says the old system was designed that way, so that the ache would remain until something could answer it.

“But deal only with food and drink and various washings, regulations for the body” — outward things, addressing the outside of a person. “Imposed until the time of reformation”, which means a setting-right, a putting straight. The old arrangement had an expiry date written into it from the beginning, and it was never meant to be permanent.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Christ appeared as a high priest of the good things that have come, then through the greater and more perfect tent (not made with hands, that is, not of this creation) he entered once for all into the holy places, not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But when Christ appeared” — and after ten verses of curtains and restrictions, the sentence breaks like a door opening.

“As a high priest of the good things that have come.” Not things that are coming. The old order dealt in anticipation; this one deals in arrival.

“Through the greater and more perfect tent (not made with hands, that is, not of this creation).” The sanctuary he passed through is not a building at all. “Not of this creation” puts it outside the whole order of made things.

“He entered once for all into the holy places.” There is the word again, ephapax, and set against verse 7 it is the whole argument. The high priest went in once a year, every year, and came out. This one went in once, and did not need to go again.

“Not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood.”

Every high priest in history walked behind that curtain carrying blood that was not his. The animal had died in his place and the man was, in the most literal sense, handling somebody else’s death. This priest brought his own — which means he had already been the victim before he was the officiant.

Note what the phrase does and does not require. “By means of his own blood” does not mean he carried a vessel of literal blood into heaven, as some have imagined. It means he entered by virtue of a death already accomplished — on the strength of his own life laid down, rather than an animal’s.

“Thus securing an eternal redemption.” Redemption is the market-place word for buying a slave out. And eternal is the letter’s standing contrast with the annual: not a release renewed each autumn but one that does not expire.

The verb means to find or obtain, with the sense of achieving something by effort. He did not receive the redemption as a gift; he went and got it, and the cost is in the previous clause.

verseByVerse.quote: For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the sprinkling of defiled persons with the ashes of a heifer, sanctify for the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For if… how much more.” The argument is from lesser to greater, and it begins by conceding that the old sacrifices genuinely worked.

“If the blood of goats and bulls, and the sprinkling of defiled persons with the ashes of a heifer, sanctify for the purification of the flesh.” The ashes of the red heifer (Num 19) were the remedy for corpse-defilement — a burnt heifer’s ashes mixed with water and sprinkled on anyone who had touched a dead body. It worked. The writer grants it without qualification.

But mark what it achieved: “purification of the flesh”. It made a man ceremonially clean and fit to enter the camp. It did not touch him.

“How much more will the blood of Christ…” and three things are said about the offering that make the comparison irresistible.

“Who through the eternal Spirit” — the whole Trinity is in the sentence: the Son offers, through the Spirit, to the Father. Whatever else Calvary was, it was not the Father doing something to an unwilling Son.

“Offered himself” — and the reflexive is the difference between this and every sacrifice before it. No animal ever volunteered. They were led, held, and killed. This victim walked to it, and the letter has already shown him praying with tears about doing so (5:7).

“Without blemish” — the technical requirement for a sacrificial animal, applied here to a moral life. Every lamb was inspected for defects; this one was inspected by enemies who wanted a charge and could not find one.

“Purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God.” And there is the answer to verse 9. What the old system could not reach, this reaches. Not the flesh but the conscience — the thing that goes on accusing after the ritual is complete.

“From dead works to serve the living God.” The contrast is exact and faintly shocking: dead works, living God. A conscience that has not been cleansed produces religion — activity performed to settle a debt, which never settles it. A cleansed conscience is released into service, which is a different thing altogether and can only be done by someone who has stopped paying.
verseByVerse.note: The ashes of a red heifer were mixed with water to cleanse anyone defiled by touching a corpse.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–28 — A Death That Reaches Backward, and a Return Without Sin
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
He is therefore the mediator of a new covenant, so that the called may receive the promised eternal inheritance, since a death has occurred redeeming them from transgressions under the first covenant (v.15). Where a will is involved the death of the maker must be established (v.16), for a will takes effect only at death (v.17) — so not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood (v.18). Moses declared every commandment and sprinkled the book and the people with blood, water, scarlet wool and hyssop (v.19), saying “This is the blood of the covenant” (v.20), and sprinkled the tent and vessels likewise (v.21); under the law almost everything is purified with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness (v.22).

So the copies were purified with these rites, but the heavenly things with better sacrifices (v.23). Christ entered not holy places made with hands but heaven itself, to appear in God’s presence on our behalf (v.24), not to offer himself repeatedly (v.25), or he would have suffered since the foundation of the world — but he has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by his own sacrifice (v.26). And as it is appointed for man to die once and after that judgement (v.27), so Christ, offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, not to deal with sin but to save those eagerly waiting for him (v.28).
verseByVerse.theology:
How the Old Testament Saints Were Saved

Christ's death redeems from transgressions committed under the first covenant. There is one way of salvation, looked forward to and looked back on.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: At Sinai the book and the people were sprinkled with the blood of the covenant.

Now: Christ will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to save those eagerly waiting for him.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance, since a death has occurred that redeems them from the transgressions committed under the first covenant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Therefore he is the mediator of a new covenant” — the theme named at 8:6, now grounded in the blood of the previous verse.

“So that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance.” Inheritance is family language, and it has been in the letter since 1:2, where the Son was appointed heir of all things. What is his by right becomes theirs by gift.

Then a clause that repays close reading: “since a death has occurred that redeems them from the transgressions committed under the first covenant.”

The death is retrospective in its reach. It deals with sins committed before it happened — the transgressions of people who lived and died under the old arrangement, whose sacrifices could not perfect the conscience.

That answers a question every thoughtful reader of the Old Testament eventually asks. If the blood of bulls and goats could not take away sins (10:4), on what basis were Abraham, Moses and David forgiven? The answer here is that they were forgiven on exactly the same basis as we are, and the payment was made afterwards.

Paul says the same thing when he writes that God passed over former sins in his divine forbearance, and demonstrated his righteousness at the cross so that he might be both just and the justifier (Rom 3:25–26). The old sacrifices were, in a sense, credit extended against a payment God intended to make. They pointed forward not merely as pictures but as promises.

So there are not two ways of salvation in Scripture, an older one by law and a newer one by grace. There is one, and everyone who has ever been saved has been saved by the same death — some looking forward to it without knowing its name, and some looking back.

“Those who are called” is the writer’s quiet word for the people in view. Not those who volunteered. The initiative is God’s in this letter as everywhere in the New Testament.

verseByVerse.quote: For where a will is involved, the death of the one who made it must be established. For a will takes effect only at death, since it is not in force as long as the one who made it is alive. Therefore not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For where a will is involved, the death of the one who made it must be established.”

The writer is making a play on a word, and it helps to know what he is doing. The Greek diatheke means both covenant and testament — a legal arrangement, and specifically a last will. He has been using it in the first sense for two chapters, and here he turns it to the second.

Some translations keep “covenant” throughout and read this as being about a covenant ratified by a representative death. The ESV takes it as a testament, and the logic of verse 17 favours that: “a will takes effect only at death, since it is not in force as long as the one who made it is alive.”

That is simply how inheritance works and always has. A will is a real document the day it is signed and it does nothing whatever. The named heirs have no claim, the estate does not move, and the whole thing waits on one event.

Apply it to the previous verse and the connection appears. Christ is the mediator, and there is a promised eternal inheritance — and an inheritance requires a death. The testator had to die before anybody could receive anything.

Which puts the cross in an unexpected light. It was not only a sacrifice offered and a penalty borne, though it was both. It was also the death that made a will operative — the moment at which an estate long promised became actually available to the heirs.

“Therefore not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood.” The writer swings back to the other sense of the word, and the two meanings are held together by a single fact: whichever way you read diatheke, somebody has to die before it operates.

And “not even” is an argument from the lesser case. If the shadow required blood, how much more the substance.
verseByVerse.note: The Greek word for “covenant” can also mean a “will,” and the writer uses both senses.

verseByVerse.quote: For when every commandment of the law had been declared by Moses to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying, “This is the blood of the covenant that God commanded for you.” And in the same way he sprinkled with the blood both the tent and all the vessels used in worship. Indeed, under the law almost everything is purified with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scene is Exodus 24, the ratification of the covenant at Sinai, and the writer describes it in some detail because he wants the blood in his readers’ eyes.

“When every commandment of the law had been declared by Moses to all the people” — the terms were read aloud first. Nobody was bound to something they had not heard.

“He took the blood of calves and goats, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people.” Hyssop was a small bushy plant used as a brush; it appears at the Passover, in the cleansing of lepers, and in David’s prayer to be purged with hyssop (Ps 51:7). And it was lifted to the cross on a stalk (John 19:29).

Exodus 24 does not mention water, scarlet wool, hyssop or the sprinkling of the book. The writer draws those details from the other cleansing rites of the law, where blood, water, scarlet yarn and hyssop belong together (Lev 14:4–7; Num 19:6), and gathers them into one picture of covenant cleansing. He adds nothing that contradicts Exodus; he shows what the ceremony at Sinai shared with the rest of the law.

Consider the scene as it would have looked: a nation standing in the open, and blood flicked over them and over the scroll of the law. The covenant document itself needed cleansing before the arrangement could stand.

“This is the blood of the covenant that God commanded for you.” Those words are worth reading twice, because the readers of this letter had heard them again in an upper room, from a man holding a cup: this is my blood of the covenant (Mark 14:24). Jesus was quoting Sinai deliberately, and telling his disciples what he was about to do.

“Under the law almost everything is purified with blood.” The “almost” is a careful touch — there were exceptions for the very poor (Lev 5:11).

“And without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins.” The principle stated flatly, and it is the sentence modern readers most resist.

It should not be softened, and it should be understood. The point is not that God is appeased by suffering, which is the pagan idea. It is that sin is not a debt that can be waived by a stroke of the pen without something being false. A God who simply overlooked evil would not be kind; he would be indifferent to the people it destroyed. Forgiveness is never free — it is free to the one forgiven, and costly to the one who forgives, and the cross is what that costs when the wrong is against God.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus it was necessary for the copies of the heavenly things to be purified with these rites, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these. For Christ has entered, not into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true things, but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf. Nor was it to offer himself repeatedly, as the high priest enters the holy places every year with blood not his own, for then he would have had to suffer repeatedly since the foundation of the world. But as it is, he has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“It was necessary for the copies of the heavenly things to be purified with these rites, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices.”

The sentence has puzzled readers: why would heavenly things need purifying? The likeliest sense is that the heavenly sanctuary required consecration for its use by sinners — not that heaven was defiled, but that access for defiled people had to be opened by blood, as the tabernacle’s use required its dedication.

“For Christ has entered not into holy places made with hands… but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf.”

That last phrase is the one to carry away. The high priest went behind the curtain representing the tribes, with their names cut into stones on his shoulders and breastpiece. This one went into the presence of God carrying us, and the word for “appear” means to be made manifest, to show oneself before someone’s face.

“Nor was it to offer himself repeatedly… for then he would have had to suffer repeatedly since the foundation of the world.”

The logic repays following, because it is a reductio. If Christ’s offering worked the way the old ones did, it would need renewing — and since sin has been in the world from the beginning, he would have been dying over and over since Eden. The absurdity proves the point: a sacrifice that has to be repeated is a sacrifice that did not work.

“But as it is, he has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.”

“The end of the ages” is where the New Testament always locates the cross — not in the middle of history but at its hinge. Everything before ran toward it; everything since runs from it.

And “put away” is a strong word: to abolish, to set aside, to annul. It is used of cancelling a law. Sin was not merely covered, as the old rites covered it. It was abolished.

verseByVerse.quote: And just as it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment, so Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, not to deal with sin but to save those who are eagerly waiting for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“It is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment.”

Two facts, stated without argument, and the writer expects no dispute about either. Death is appointed — it is not an accident of biology but an appointment kept. And something follows it.

“Once” is doing work here beyond the obvious. It rules out any scheme of repeated lives, and more importantly it establishes the pattern the next verse needs: one death, then the reckoning.

Is there a second chance after death, or a purgatory where believers are purified? This verse leaves no room for either. Death is followed by judgment, not by a further opportunity. Roman Catholic teaching holds that many believers must be cleansed after death before they enter heaven. But this letter says that by his single offering Christ has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (10:14), and that leaves nothing to be paid afterward. Believers too will stand before God, but for them the verdict was given at the cross; what remains is the review of their lives for reward (2 Cor 5:10), not a sentence to be served.

“So Christ” — and the parallel is the point of the whole sentence. He follows the human pattern exactly. Offered once, and then what comes after.

“Having been offered once to bear the sins of many.” The verb is Isaiah’s — he bore the sin of many (Isa 53:12) — and it means to carry up, to take a weight onto oneself. Not to sympathise with sinners but to shoulder what they owed.

Does many mean that Christ bore the sins of only some? The word comes from Isaiah 53:12, where it sets the one servant against the great number he saves. Many Christians take it to mean simply that his death was for the multitude; Reformed Christians take it to mean that he actually bore the sins of a definite people, all who will be saved. The second is the more likely, since to bear sin is to carry it away, and those whose sins he carried will never have to bear them (cf. 2:9). Either way, many is not few, and the invitation is to all.

“Will appear a second time.” And here the parallel turns, because what follows his death is not judgement for him. He has been judged already, in our place.

“Not to deal with sin” — and that phrase deserves to be underlined for anyone who is afraid of the second coming. The sin business is finished. He is not returning to reopen the file, to weigh his people again, or to see whether the first visit took. That work was completed and he sat down.

“But to save those who are eagerly waiting for him.” The word means to wait eagerly and expectantly, like someone watching a road. It is the same idea as Paul’s crown for all who have loved his appearing (2 Tim 4:8).

And that is the description of a Christian this chapter ends on, after all the blood and curtains and ashes: someone standing at the window, looking down the road, waiting for a man who has already dealt with everything that could have made the waiting frightening.

10.title: Once for All: The New and Living Way
10.overview:
Chapter 10 is the theological summit toward which the entire central argument of Hebrews has been climbing. The priestly argument (chs. 5–7), the covenant argument (ch. 8), and the sacrificial argument (ch. 9) all converge here. The shadow of the law, with its annual repetition of animal sacrifice, is contrasted one final time with the once-for-all offering of Christ, this time with Psalm 40 as the key text: “I have come to do your will, O God.” The Father prepared a body for the Son; the Son offered that body in perfect obedience; and by that single offering “we have been sanctified” — permanently, definitively, without need of repetition.

With the theological argument complete, the letter pivots to its longest pastoral application (vv. 19–39). Three great imperatives flow from the three gifts of the new covenant: draw near to God (the open access secured by Christ’s blood), hold fast the confession (the settled certainty of God’s promises), and stir up one another to love and good works (the communal life of the Spirit). These are not three separate duties; they are three faces of the same gospel-shaped life: toward God, toward his word, toward one another.

The fourth warning passage (vv. 26–31) is the most severe in the letter. But it is immediately balanced by the most extended encouragement yet (vv. 32–39): remember the early days, the public suffering you endured, the property you lost with joy. You have already run a hard stretch of the race. You need endurance for just a little while more. “Yet a little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay.” The return of Christ is the horizon toward which the whole chapter is pointed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — One Sacrifice, and a Priest Who Sat Down
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The law has only a shadow of the good things to come, and can never by the same annual sacrifices perfect those who draw near (v.1) — otherwise they would have ceased, since the cleansed would have no more consciousness of sins (v.2). Instead there is a reminder of sins every year (v.3), for it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take them away (v.4).

So when Christ came into the world he said, in the words of Psalm 40: sacrifices you have not desired, but a body you have prepared for me (v.5); in burnt offerings you have taken no pleasure (v.6); behold, I have come to do your will (v.7). Having said the first (v.8), he then adds the second — doing away with the one to establish the other (v.9); and by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all (v.10).

Every priest stands daily, offering the same sacrifices which can never take away sins (v.11); but Christ, having offered one sacrifice for all time, sat down at God’s right hand (v.12), waiting until his enemies are made a footstool (v.13) — for by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (v.14). The Holy Spirit bears witness (v.15), quoting the new covenant promise (v.16) and its close: I will remember their sins no more (v.17). And where there is forgiveness, there is no longer any offering for sin (v.18).
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Tenses in One Sentence

By a single offering Christ has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified. Where sins are forgiven, there is no longer any offering for sin.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The yearly sacrifices were a reminder of sins, and their repetition confessed that they had not finished the work.

Now: Standing before God does not wait on our progress; our progress flows from a finished offering.

verseByVerse.quote: For since the law has but a shadow of the good things to come instead of the true form of these realities, it can never, by the same sacrifices that are continually offered every year, make perfect those who draw near. Otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered, since the worshipers, having once been cleansed, would no longer have any consciousness of sins?
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The law has but a shadow of the good things to come instead of the true form of these realities.”

The shadow image returns from 8:5, and the second term sharpens it. “True form” is eikon — the image, the actual likeness. The contrast is not between a shadow and nothing but between a shadow and the thing that casts it.

A shadow tells you something real. It tells you a body is there, roughly how tall, roughly what shape. It does not tell you the face, and you cannot shake hands with it.

“It can never, by the same sacrifices that are continually offered every year, make perfect those who draw near.” Never — the writer is not describing a system that worked imperfectly but one that could not, in principle, finish the job.

Then verse 2, and it is a piece of plain reasoning that any worshipper could have done for himself: “Otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered?”

The repetition is the evidence. If the Day of Atonement had actually dealt with the matter, there would have been no need for another one the following autumn. The fact that the calendar came round again every year was itself a confession that nothing had been concluded.

“Since the worshipers, having once been cleansed, would no longer have any consciousness of sins.”

And there is the test the writer applies, and it is an experiential one. A sacrifice that had truly worked would leave a person without a nagging sense of guilt — not because he had become forgetful or hardened, but because the thing had been genuinely settled.

Put that plainly to any religious system, including the ones people build for themselves inside Christianity. If a person is still trying to quiet the same accusation this year that he was trying to quiet last year, the method is not working, and the repetition is the proof.

verseByVerse.quote: But in these sacrifices there is a reminder of sins every year. For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But in these sacrifices there is a reminder of sins every year.”

This is one of the most penetrating observations in the letter, and it inverts what you would expect. The Day of Atonement is usually thought of as the day sins were dealt with. The writer says its actual effect was to bring them to mind.

Picture the ceremony. The high priest lays both hands on the head of the live goat and confesses over it all the iniquities of the people, and the goat is led away into the wilderness (Lev 16:21). The whole nation stands and hears its sins recited. That is not an annual clearing of the books. It is an annual reading of them aloud.

And the effect was cumulative. Every year the same ceremony, every year the same confession, every year the reminder that last year’s had not held. A devout Israelite grew old watching the same goat led out into the desert and knowing the priest would be doing it again next autumn.

Then verse 4 states the reason with a bluntness that must have startled the first hearers: “For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.”

Impossible — the same absolute word as 6:4 and 6:18. Not inadequate, not partial. It cannot be done, and it never could.

Consider what a sentence that is to write to people who were being drawn back to the temple, and what it says about the whole sacrificial system God himself commanded. The writer is not accusing anyone of doing it wrongly. He is saying the mechanism was never capable of the result.

And the reason is not hard to see once stated. Sin is a personal and moral matter between a creature and his Maker, and an animal is neither a person nor a moral agent. It has done nothing and consented to nothing. A creature that cannot understand the transaction cannot conduct it.

So what were the sacrifices for? Everything the letter has said supplies the answer. They were the shadow — teaching a nation for fourteen centuries that sin costs life, that God provides the victim, and that somebody innocent dies in the place of somebody guilty. They were a language being taught, so that when the reality came there would be words to describe it.

Were Old Testament believers forgiven, then? Yes, truly forgiven, but not by the animals. They were forgiven by God’s grace through faith, on the credit of the sacrifice Christ would offer: his death redeems them from the transgressions committed under the first covenant (9:15; cf. Rom 3:25). The sacrifices were the means God gave for their faith to lay hold of his promise, not the ground of their pardon.

verseByVerse.quote: Consequently, when Christ came into the world, he said, “Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body have you prepared for me; in burnt offerings and sin offerings you have taken no pleasure. Then I said, ’Behold, I have come to do your will, O God, as it is written of me in the scroll of the book.’”
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Consequently, when Christ came into the world, he said…” The writer puts Psalm 40 on the lips of the incarnate Son, at the moment of his coming — and it is a striking piece of interpretation. He hears the psalm as the Son’s own words to the Father about why he came.

“Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired.” The Old Testament says this repeatedly, and it is easy to misread. God commanded the sacrifices; he cannot be renouncing his own institution. The prophets say the same thing in the same idiom — I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice (Hos 6:6) — and the meaning is comparative: not these, but something they were pointing toward.

“But a body have you prepared for me.” Here is a detail worth knowing. The Hebrew of Psalm 40:6 reads “ears you have dug for me” — an odd phrase, probably meaning ears opened to hear and obey. The Greek translation the writer uses reads “a body you have prepared for me”.

The two are not at odds. An ear is the organ of obedience, and the writer’s point is the same either way: what God wanted was not an animal but a life at his disposal. The Greek simply makes explicit what the Hebrew implies, and it lands with peculiar force in a letter about the incarnation. God did not want a body brought to the altar. He prepared one, and it walked there.

“Behold, I have come to do your will, O God.” That is the sentence the writer will build on, and notice what it contains and what it does not. No bargaining, no conditions, no mention of the cost. Just arrival and willingness.

“As it is written of me in the scroll of the book.” The Son is described as coming to fulfil something already written about him. Whatever else this implies, it means the incarnation was not a rescue plan improvised after things went wrong. It was in the book.

And the whole quotation answers a question the chapter has raised. If bulls and goats cannot take away sins, what can? The answer is not a better animal. It is a will — a human will, in a prepared body, saying yes.
verseByVerse.note: “A body have you prepared for me” follows the Greek Old Testament; the Hebrew of Ps 40:6 reads “you have given me an open ear.”

verseByVerse.quote: When he said above, “You have neither desired nor taken pleasure in sacrifices and offerings and burnt offerings and sin offerings” (these are offered according to the law), then he added, “Behold, I have come to do your will.” He does away with the first in order to establish the second. And by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The writer now takes his own quotation apart, and the method repays watching, because it is how the New Testament reads the Old.

“When he said above… then he added…” he divides the psalm into two statements and puts them in order. First a negative: God did not desire sacrifices and offerings. Then a positive: behold, I have come to do your will.

“He does away with the first in order to establish the second.”

The conclusion is drawn from the sequence itself. The two statements stand side by side in the psalm, and the order is not accidental — the second is offered as the replacement for the first. You do not announce what you have come to do unless something else is being set aside.

“Does away with” is a strong verb: to take up and remove, to abolish. And “establish” is its opposite — to make stand. One thing is taken down so that another can be set up in its place, and both actions are the Son’s.

Then verse 10, which is the summit of the chapter: “And by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.”

Take the phrases in turn. “By that will” — the will of God, which the Son came to do. What sanctifies us is not our willing but his.

“We have been sanctified” — and the tense should stop any reader who has spent years anxious about his own progress. It is the Greek perfect: completed, with the result standing. Not we are being sanctified, not we hope to be. It has happened.

The letter is not confusing this with the daily business of becoming holy — verse 14 will speak of “those who are being sanctified” in the same breath. Both are true, and the order matters enormously: a Christian is set apart definitively by what Christ did, and is then progressively made to match it. The second is a lifetime’s work. The first is finished.

“Once for all.” Ephapax again, and it is the word the whole letter has been driving toward.

verseByVerse.quote: And every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God, waiting from that time until his enemies should be made a footstool for his feet. For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Every priest stands daily at his service.” One word, and the writer has been preparing it since 1:3.

There were no chairs in the tabernacle. Not one — the furniture is listed in detail in Exodus and no seat appears, because a priest whose work was finished was a contradiction in terms. They stood, every day, for fourteen centuries.

“Offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins.” The verdict of verse 4 restated, now with the emphasis on the endlessness. Same sacrifices, same priest, same standing, same result.

“But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down.”

There is the contrast, and it is made entirely with a posture. Everything the letter wants to say about the finality of the cross is carried by a man sitting down in a building that had no chairs.

“Waiting from that time until his enemies should be made a footstool.” Psalm 110:1 once more. He is seated and he is waiting — which tells you where we are in the story. The work of atonement is over; the subduing of enemies is not, and the letter’s readers were feeling the difference.

Then verse 14, and it is one of the sentences to write on the inside of the skull: “For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified.”

Two tenses in one sentence, and holding them together is the whole Christian life. Perfected — perfect tense, done, complete, and “for all time” removes any question of expiry. Being sanctified — present, continuous, unfinished, still in progress this morning.

The same people are described both ways at once. In God’s sight, on the basis of one offering, they are already finished. In their own experience they are halfway through and struggling.

Get those the wrong way round and the Christian life becomes unbearable: a person who thinks his standing depends on his progress will never rest, and a person who thinks his progress does not matter has not understood what he was set apart for. The letter puts them in the right order, in a single sentence, and never separates them.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Holy Spirit also bears witness to us; for after saying, “This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws on their hearts, and write them on their minds,” then he adds, “I will remember their sins and their lawless deeds no more.” Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And the Holy Spirit also bears witness to us.” Present tense again, as at 3:7. The Jeremiah passage quoted at length in chapter 8 is now brought back in shortened form, and it is introduced as testimony being given now, in the room.

Note that the writer quotes only two clauses of it, and which two. He leaves out the promise that all shall know the Lord, and the covenant formula about being their God. He takes the law written on hearts, and the sins remembered no more.

That is not carelessness. He is quoting for a purpose, and the purpose arrives in verse 18.

“I will remember their sins and their lawless deeds no more.” The promise from 8:12, and the writer now does something with it that he did not do there. He draws an inference.

“Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin.”

The logic is inescapable once stated. If God has undertaken never to bring up a person’s sins again, then there is nothing left for a sacrifice to do. An offering exists to deal with an outstanding matter. Where the matter is closed, the offering is not merely unnecessary — it is unintelligible.

And that is the writer’s decisive argument against the thing his readers were contemplating. Going back to the temple would not be a harmless supplement or a matter of ancestral loyalty. It would be to keep offering for sins that God has said he will not remember, which is to imply the promise is not true.

The verse also settles a question that has divided Christians. If there is no longer any offering for sin, then whatever the church does when it gathers, it is not offering a sacrifice for sin. The New Testament knows sacrifices of praise and of doing good (13:15-16) and calls a Christian’s body a living sacrifice (Rom 12:1). It knows no repeatable offering for sin, and this verse is why.

With that the great doctrinal argument of the letter is complete. From here the writer turns to what his readers must do about it, and the next verse begins “therefore”.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–39 — Let Us Draw Near, Hold Fast, and Consider One Another
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Therefore, since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus (v.19), by the new and living way opened through the curtain, that is, his flesh (v.20), and a great priest over God’s house (v.21) — let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, hearts sprinkled clean and bodies washed (v.22); let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who promised is faithful (v.23); and let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works (v.24), not neglecting to meet together as some do, but encouraging one another all the more as the Day draws near (v.25).

For if we go on sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, no sacrifice for sins remains (v.26), but a fearful expectation of judgement (v.27). Anyone setting aside Moses’ law died without mercy on two or three witnesses (v.28); how much worse for one who has trampled the Son of God, profaned the blood of the covenant and outraged the Spirit of grace (v.29)? For we know him who said, vengeance is mine, and the Lord will judge his people (v.30) — and it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God (v.31).

But recall the former days: after being enlightened you endured a hard struggle (v.32), publicly exposed to reproach, and partners with those so treated (v.33); you had compassion on prisoners and joyfully accepted the plundering of your property, knowing you had a better and abiding possession (v.34). So do not throw away your confidence, which has a great reward (v.35); you have need of endurance, to receive what is promised (v.36). For yet a little while and the coming one will come (v.37); my righteous one shall live by faith, and if he shrinks back my soul has no pleasure in him (v.38). But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls (v.39).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Curtain Is His Flesh

The way into the holy places has been opened through the curtain, his flesh. So draw near, hold fast because he who promised is faithful, and stir one another up.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: These believers had once joyfully accepted the plundering of their property.

Now: The warning of verses 26–31 is aimed at deliberate repudiation of Christ, not at a struggling believer; and it ends in assurance: we are not of those who shrink back.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh, and since we have a great priest over the house of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Therefore, brothers” — and the letter turns. Nine chapters of argument now become three exhortations, and everything from here rests on what has been proved.

“Since we have confidence to enter the holy places.” The word is parresia, as at 4:16 — the free citizen’s right to speak openly. And the place named is the one the whole letter has been circling: the room behind the curtain, which one man entered once a year and everybody else never.

“By the blood of Jesus.” That is the ground, and it is the only one offered. Not by sincerity, not by improvement, not by a life that has earned an audience.

“By the new and living way that he opened for us.” The word for new means fresh, recent; and “living” is the arresting adjective: not a road but a way that is alive, because it is a person.

“Through the curtain, that is, through his flesh.”

The identification is startling and it repays sitting with. The curtain was the barrier — the thing that kept people out. And the writer says the curtain is his flesh.

Which means the way in was opened by the tearing of it. When Jesus died, the temple veil was torn from top to bottom (Mark 15:38), and the Gospels record it as an act done from above rather than below. His body was rent, and the barrier with it.

There is a further note in it that the readers would have felt. The curtain was beautiful — blue and purple and scarlet, worked with cherubim. The barrier between God and man was not ugly. It was magnificent, and it had to be destroyed.

“And since we have a great priest over the house of God.” The second ground: not only an open way but a man standing at the end of it who belongs to us. “Over the house” recalls 3:6, where Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son — and we are that house.

verseByVerse.quote: let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Let us draw near.” The first of the three exhortations, and it is the letter’s central verb — the priestly word, used of what only priests could do, now commanded of everybody.

Four qualifications follow, and they divide into two pairs: two about the person coming, two about what has been done to him.

“With a true heart” — a genuine one, without pretence. This rules out the approach that keeps something back, and it also rules out coming in somebody else’s borrowed words. God is not interested in a performance at the throne.

“In full assurance of faith” — the same phrase as 6:11, meaning carried to complete conviction. Not certainty about oneself, which nobody has, but certainty about the ground just described: the blood, the way, the priest.

Then the second pair, and both verbs are passive — things done to us rather than by us.

“With our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience.” The image is the sprinkling that consecrated priests at their ordination (Exod 29:21), and the target is the conscience again — the thing 9:9 said the old sacrifices could not reach. What accuses a man on the inside has been dealt with, and that is why he can come with a true heart rather than a defended one.

“And our bodies washed with pure water.” Priests were also washed at their ordination, and most readers hear an allusion to baptism here as well. Whether or not the writer intended that, the pairing is deliberate: inward cleansing and outward, the whole person made fit.

The more likely reading is that the writer does mean baptism, as the outward sign of the inward cleansing he names in the same breath. The picture draws on the washing of the priests (Exod 29:4) and on God’s promise, I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean (Ezek 36:25). Some read the washing as purely figurative, a picture of moral cleansing. But even if baptism is in view, the water does not do the cleansing. The heart is sprinkled clean by Christ’s blood; baptism is the sign of it, given to those who have drawn near in faith (cf. 1 Pet 3:21).

Put the four together and notice what is not among them. There is no requirement of worthiness, no interval of preparation, no measure of progress. Every qualification is either an attitude of honesty or something Christ has already done — which is exactly the point, because a throne you must qualify for is not a throne of grace.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who promised is faithful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering.” The second exhortation, and it is the one aimed most directly at these readers’ situation.

“The confession” is the word from 3:1 and 4:14 — what they had said publicly, probably at baptism, and were under pressure to unsay. In a hostile city a confession is not a private opinion; it is the thing that got their property confiscated.

“Hold fast” means grip, retain, do not let go. And “without wavering” is a single word meaning not leaning, not tilting — the picture is of something that stays upright rather than swaying between two positions.

Then the reason, and it is one short clause carrying the whole weight: “for he who promised is faithful.”

Read it carefully, because the logic is not the one we would supply. He does not say hold on because you are strong, or because you have held on so far, or because giving up would be shameful. The ground of our holding is his faithfulness.

That is the difference between Christian perseverance and mere determination. A man gritting his teeth is relying on his grip, and grips fail. A man holding fast because the promiser is faithful is relying on something outside himself, and the holding on is a response to reliability rather than a substitute for it.

Notice too what is held: the confession of our hope. Not of our feelings, which come and go, and not of our achievements. Hope is by definition about something not yet in hand, which is why holding it requires anything at all.

And this is the answer to the drift of 2:1. A congregation slipping away is not usually losing an argument; it is losing its grip in the dark. The writer does not give them a new argument. He points at the character of the one who made the promise, and tells them to hang on to that.

verseByVerse.quote: And let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day drawing near.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works.” The third exhortation, and it turns outward. The first two were about our approach to God; this one is about each other.

“Consider” is the verb from 3:1, where it was applied to Jesus — to fix the mind on, to study attentively. Here it is applied to other Christians. Working out how to help a particular person forward requires the same kind of attention as contemplating Christ, and the writer uses the same word for both.

“Stir up” is a startling choice. The noun is paroxysmos, from which we get paroxysm; it means a sharp provoking, an irritation. It is the word Luke uses of the bitter quarrel between Paul and Barnabas (Acts 15:39).

So the instruction is to provoke one another — and the only thing that redeems it is the object. Provoke, yes, but to love and good works. There is a kind of friction between Christians that is entirely legitimate: the friend who will not let you settle, whose example makes your comfort uncomfortable.

“Not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some.” And here is the first concrete symptom the letter has named. The drift of 2:1 and the dullness of 5:11 have a visible expression: people had stopped coming.

Note that it is called a habit. Not a decision, not a repudiation. A pattern that had established itself, which is exactly how drifting works.

And the reasons would have been good ones. Meeting was dangerous; assembling with Christians marked you out in a city that had already plundered their property. Staying away was prudent. The writer names it anyway, because the previous verses have just made attendance the mechanism of everything else — you cannot stir up one another, or be stirred, from a distance.

Does watching a service online fulfil this command? The word is about gathering, being together in one place, and the stirring up it describes needs people who are present to each other. For the sick, the housebound and those cut off by persecution, a livestream is a real mercy, and no one should be made to feel guilty for what they cannot help. But for those who can come, watching is not meeting, and a settled habit of staying away is exactly the drift this verse warns against.

“But encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day drawing near.” The instinct under pressure is to withdraw and go quiet. The letter says the opposite: the nearer the Day and the harder the times, the more of this, not less.

verseByVerse.quote: For if we go on sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, but a fearful expectation of judgment, and a fury of fire that will consume the adversaries.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For if we go on sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins.”

The fourth warning, and it must be read with the same care as chapter 6 — and with attention to the words the writer actually chose.

“Deliberately” stands first in the Greek sentence, in the emphatic position. And the phrase is a technical one. The law distinguished sins committed unintentionally, for which sacrifice was provided (Lev 4), from sin done “with a high hand”, for which there was no offering at all and the sinner was cut off (Num 15:30–31). The writer is using that category, and his readers would have recognised it instantly.

“Go on sinning” is a present participle: continuing, persisting. Not a fall but a settled course.

“After receiving the knowledge of the truth” — with full information. This is not the sin of the ignorant or the deceived.

Put those together and the sin in view is specific: the informed, deliberate, persistent repudiation of Christ by someone who knows exactly what he is walking away from. Verse 29 will describe it in the plainest terms — trampling the Son of God underfoot.

“There no longer remains a sacrifice for sins.” And the logic is the same as verse 18, running the other way. There is one sacrifice, offered once. A person who rejects it has not exhausted a supply; he has refused the only one there is, and there is no second provision behind it.

This should be said plainly for the comfort of the anxious, because these verses have terrified people they were never aimed at. The passage does not describe a Christian who has sinned badly, or repeatedly, or who is fighting a besetting sin and losing. Such a person has a sacrifice, and the whole letter has been urging him to come and use it. It describes someone who has looked at the sacrifice and trampled on it.

“But a fearful expectation of judgment, and a fury of fire.” The language is Isaiah’s (Isa 26:11), and the word for adversaries makes the point: this is what awaits enemies, not stumbling sons.

verseByVerse.quote: Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the evidence of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by the one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and has profaned the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and has outraged the Spirit of grace? For we know him who said, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay.” And again, “The Lord will judge his people.” It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The argument runs again from lesser to greater, as at 2:2.

“Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the evidence of two or three witnesses.” That is Deuteronomy 17:6, and the offence in view there is idolatry — going and serving other gods. The penalty was death, and the safeguard was witnesses.

“How much worse punishment, do you think…” The writer puts it as a question and invites his readers to do the arithmetic themselves.

Three descriptions follow, and they escalate.

“Has trampled underfoot the Son of God” — not merely rejected but treated with contempt, walked on. “Has profaned the blood of the covenant” — the verb means to treat as common, to reckon something holy as ordinary. “And has outraged the Spirit of grace” — insulted, treated with insolence.

The phrase “by which he was sanctified” has been much debated, since it appears to describe the apostate as having been sanctified by the blood. It most likely means set apart in the external sense — he belonged to the covenant community and was marked out by it, as Israel was sanctified at Sinai. That is consistent with everything the letter says elsewhere, and with the field in 6:7–8 that drank the same rain.

Can a true believer fall into this? Christians answer in three main ways. Arminians hold that a real believer can turn away and be lost, and they point to the strong words here: he was sanctified by the blood. Some take the warning as hypothetical, describing what would happen if a believer fell away, though God will not let it happen. Others hold that the writer describes someone who belonged to the covenant community, knew the truth and shared its privileges, but never truly trusted Christ, and at last walked away (cf. 6:4–8). The last is the more likely, and the letter itself points that way. It says of its readers, we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed (10:39), and it rests their perseverance on Christ, who saves to the uttermost (7:25). God keeps his own, and warnings like this one are among the means he uses to do it.

“For we know him who said, Vengeance is mine.” Two quotations from Deuteronomy 32, and the second is the sharper: “The Lord will judge his people.” Not the nations. His people. Belonging to the covenant community is not a shelter from God’s judgement; it is the reason judgement begins there (cf. 1 Pet 4:17).

“It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.”

And note the phrase, because it is the letter’s own and it cuts both ways. To fall away is to fall away from the living God (3:12) — and there is nowhere to fall except into his hands. The same hands are the only refuge and the only danger, and which they are depends entirely on how a man comes.

verseByVerse.quote: But recall the former days when, after you were enlightened, you endured a hard struggle with sufferings, sometimes being publicly exposed to reproach and affliction, and sometimes being partners with those so treated. For you had compassion on those in prison, and you joyfully accepted the plundering of your property, since you knew that you yourselves had a better possession and an abiding one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But recall the former days” — and the tone changes completely. Having brought them to the edge, the writer turns and reminds them who they are.

This is the most valuable historical paragraph in the letter, because it tells us what had actually happened to these people.

“After you were enlightened, you endured a hard struggle with sufferings.” The word for struggle is athlesis, the athletic contest word. And note the timing: the suffering came after the light, not before. Becoming Christians is what brought it on them.

“Sometimes being publicly exposed to reproach and affliction.” The verb is a theatre word — made a spectacle of, put on a stage. Public humiliation, in a culture where honour and shame were the currency of a life.

“And sometimes being partners with those so treated.” Which took its own kind of courage. It is one thing to be dragged out yourself; it is another to walk over and stand beside somebody who has been, when you could have stayed indoors.

“For you had compassion on those in prison.” Visiting a prisoner in that world meant identifying yourself publicly with his crime, and prisoners depended on visitors for food. These people went.

“And you joyfully accepted the plundering of your property.”

Read that twice. Not endured. Not tolerated. Joyfully accepted — while their houses were being emptied, presumably by neighbours, with no legal recourse whatever.

“Since you knew that you yourselves had a better possession and an abiding one.” And there is how they did it. Not by stoicism or by pretending the loss was small. By knowing they owned something the mob could not reach and could not carry.

The word “abiding” is the letter’s word for what lasts, set against everything that wears out like a garment (1:11). These people had once made that calculation under real pressure and come out singing — which is precisely why the writer reminds them. He is not asking them to become something new. He is asking them to be what they already were.
verseByVerse.note: Possibly the persecution under the emperor Claudius, who expelled Jews from Rome about AD 49.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not throw away your confidence, which has a great reward. For you have need of endurance, so that when you have done the will of God you may receive what is promised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Therefore do not throw away your confidence.”

The verb is deliberate and slightly shocking. Not “do not lose” it, as though it might slip out of a pocket. To throw away is an act — you do it on purpose, the way a soldier throws away a shield to run faster.

And “confidence” is parresia, the same word as verse 19 and 4:16: the boldness to speak, the freedom to come. What they are in danger of discarding is not a mood but their access.

The word was also used of the frankness that could get a man into trouble in a public assembly. There is a version of quietness that looks like humility and is actually the shield going over the wall.

“Which has a great reward.” The writer is not embarrassed by the motive. He has told them their possession is better and abiding (v.34), and here he says the boldness itself is worth keeping because of what it earns. Reward-language runs through this letter (11:6, 11:26) and it is never treated as a lower motive.

“For you have need of endurance.” A plain sentence, and notice what it concedes. Not need of better arguments, or clearer teaching, or a fresh experience. Endurance — hypomone, remaining under a weight without buckling.

That is the writer’s diagnosis after ten chapters of theology, and it is a humbling one for anyone who assumes that people leave the faith because they have run out of reasons. These readers had the reasons. What they were short of was staying power.

“So that when you have done the will of God you may receive what is promised.” And note the order. Doing comes first and receiving after — not because the promise is earned, but because it lies at the end of a road that must actually be walked. Endurance is not waiting; it is continuing to obey while nothing visible changes.

verseByVerse.quote: For, “Yet a little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay; but my righteous one shall live by faith, and if he shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The writer quotes Habakkuk, and he has chosen the passage with care, because Habakkuk is the prophet of waiting. His book opens with the complaint: how long, O LORD, and you will not hear? The answer he received was that the vision awaits its appointed time; if it seems slow, wait for it (Hab 2:3).

“Yet a little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay.” The Greek reads literally “a little while, how little, how little” — a doubling that presses the shortness. And where Habakkuk’s Hebrew speaks of the vision coming, the Greek text the writer follows speaks of a person — “the coming one”.

“But my righteous one shall live by faith.” It is the sentence that changed Luther’s life and Paul builds two letters on it (Rom 1:17; Gal 3:11). Hebrews uses it differently, and the difference is instructive.

Paul takes it to answer the question how is a man justified — by faith, not works. Hebrews takes it to answer how does a man keep going — by faith, not sight. The emphasis here falls on live: the righteous man does not merely begin by faith, he lives by it, day after day, and the whole of chapter 11 is about to illustrate what that looks like over a lifetime.

“And if he shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him.” The verb means to draw back, to withdraw — it was used of furling a sail and of a man shrinking from danger. Paul uses it of himself at Miletus: I did not shrink from declaring the whole counsel of God (Acts 20:27).

And the contrast is exact. Faith goes forward when it cannot see; shrinking back is what faith looks like when it fails. The wilderness generation shrank back at the border of a good land, and it is the same failure of nerve.

“My soul has no pleasure in him” is a restrained way of saying something severe, and its restraint is characteristic of Scripture at its most serious. It is not rage. It is the withdrawal of delight, which from God is worse.

verseByVerse.quote: But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls.”

The chapter that contains the letter’s most frightening warning ends with the writer putting himself and his readers firmly on the right side of it — and the placing is deliberate.

“We” — he includes himself, as he has done again and again since 2:1. And “are not of those” is a statement of category, not of achievement. He is not saying we have performed better. He is saying we belong to a different kind.

This is how the warnings in Hebrews are meant to work, and the pattern repays learning, because it recurs. The writer describes the danger in the strongest terms available, and then tells his readers he does not believe it applies to them — exactly as he did at 6:9 after the harshest passage in the letter. Warning and assurance are not alternatives here. The warning is one of the means by which the assurance turns out to be true.

“Shrink back and are destroyed” — the word means ruin, loss — the same word as Philippians 3:19, “their end is destruction”. Set against it is “preserve their souls”, literally the gaining or keeping of the soul, an idiom for coming through alive.

And the two categories are defined by one thing only, which the writer names last: faith. Not endurance, though he has just demanded it; not good works, though he has commended theirs. Faith is what distinguishes those who arrive from those who turn back.

Which is exactly why the next chapter is what it is. Having said that the difference between destruction and preservation is faith, the writer immediately defines it — and then spends forty verses producing a crowd of people who had it, so that a struggling congregation could see what the word looks like when it is worn by real men and women over a lifetime.
