11.title: By Faith: The Great Cloud of Witnesses
11.overview:
Chapter 11 is one of the most beloved passages in all of Scripture — the great gallery of faith, a sweeping movement through salvation history that shows what it looks like to live by trust in what is not yet visible. The writer has spent ten chapters making the theological case for the all-sufficiency of Jesus; now he demonstrates it experimentally, showing that the saints of the Old Testament were sustained through their entire lives by faith in the promises of God — promises they received, embraced, and died without fully receiving. They were looking forward to what we have received. Their faith and ours are one continuous movement toward the one promised city.

The definition of faith in verse 1 is not a philosophical proposition but a practical description: “the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen.” Faith is not a leap in the dark or an act of wishful thinking; it is the settled confidence that what God has promised is more real than what can be seen and touched, precisely because it is grounded in God’s character and sworn by his oath. It is, as the writer has shown in chapters 1–10, a reasonable response to the evidence: the evidence of the Son, the better covenant, the better sacrifice, the permanent intercession.

The chapter’s theological climax comes at the end: “And all these, though commended through their faith, did not receive what was promised, since God had provided something better for us, that apart from us they should not be made perfect.” The Old Testament saints were not left behind. They are not inferior. They are incomplete without us — and we are incomplete without them. The entire company of the redeemed, across all the ages, will together receive the fullness of the promise. This is the most moving vision of the solidarity of the saints in all of Scripture.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — By Faith: Title Deeds and Tents
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen (v.1), by which the people of old were commended (v.2) — and by which we understand that the universe was made by God’s word, so that the visible did not come from the visible (v.3). By faith Abel offered a better sacrifice and still speaks though dead (v.4); Enoch was taken without seeing death, commended as having pleased God (v.5) — and without faith it is impossible to please him, for whoever draws near must believe that he is and that he rewards those who seek him (v.6). By faith Noah built an ark for events as yet unseen (v.7).

By faith Abraham obeyed and went out not knowing where he was going (v.8), living in tents in the land of promise with Isaac and Jacob (v.9), looking for the city with foundations whose builder is God (v.10). By faith Sarah received power to conceive, considering him faithful who had promised (v.11), so that from one man as good as dead came descendants like the stars and the sand (v.12).

These all died in faith without receiving the promises, having greeted them from afar as strangers and exiles (v.13) — and people who speak so are seeking a homeland (v.14); had they meant the land they left, they could have returned (v.15), but they desire a better, heavenly country, so God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared them a city (v.16). By faith Abraham offered Isaac (v.17), of whom it was said the offspring would be named (v.18), reckoning that God could raise him (v.19). By faith Isaac blessed (v.20), Jacob worshipped over his staff (v.21), and Joseph gave directions about his bones (v.22).
verseByVerse.theology:
Faith as a Title Deed

Faith gives the things hoped for a footing in the present, because it rests on the reliability of the one who promised. Everyone in this gallery is commended for something they did that made no sense apart from God's word.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob lived in tents in the land of promise and died without receiving it.

Now: God is not ashamed to be called the God of people who are visibly waiting for a better country.

verseByVerse.quote: Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen. For by it the people of old received their commendation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen.”

It is not quite a definition. The writer is not saying what faith is in the abstract; he is saying what faith does, and the two nouns repay pressing.

“Assurance” is hypostasis — literally that which stands under, a substructure. The same word was used at 1:3 of the very being of God. In the papyri it appears in property documents for a title deed, the paper that establishes a claim to something you do not yet hold.

That is a remarkable thing to say about faith. It does not merely wish for the things hoped for; it gives them a footing in the present. A man with a title deed to a house he has never seen owns it, and behaves accordingly.

“Conviction” is elenchos, a word from the law courts — proof, evidence, the demonstration that settles a case. Faith functions as evidence of what cannot be seen.

Both words guard against a misunderstanding that has done real damage. Faith in Hebrews is not a leap in the dark, and it is not believing without grounds. It is the settled confidence that treats God’s word as the evidence it is — because the ground of faith is not the strength of the believing but the reliability of the promiser (10:23).

Note also what faith is directed toward: things hoped for and things not seen. Both are about the invisible and the future, which is exactly the difficulty these readers were in. They could see the temple, the neighbours, the empty houses. What they could not see was the thing they had been promised.

“For by it the people of old received their commendation.” The word means to be witnessed to, well spoken of — and it recurs through the chapter (vv. 4, 5, 39). God himself is the one bearing witness. The whole gallery that follows exists to show that this is what he approves.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God, so that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“By faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God.”

The first example is not a person, and the choice is deliberate. Before Abel, before Noah, before Abraham, the writer begins with the whole congregation and something every one of them believes.

And note the pairing: faith and understand. They are not opposites here. Faith is presented as the faculty by which something is genuinely known — not a substitute for understanding but the means of it.

“The universe was created by the word of God.” Which is exactly how Genesis tells it: God said, and it was. Nothing was worked with, shaped, or wrestled into form. He spoke.

The verse teaches that God made the world out of nothing, by speaking. It does not say how long he took. That is settled by Genesis itself, whose plainest reading, confirmed in the fourth commandment, is six ordinary days: For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth (Exod 20:11).

“So that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible.” The visible world does not have a visible origin. Trace it back as far as you like and you do not arrive at earlier stuff; you arrive at a word.

Why start here? Because the chapter is about acting on the strength of what cannot be seen, and creation is the first and largest instance. Nobody watched it happen. There were no witnesses, and there is no possibility of any. Every person who believes the world was made does so on the strength of testimony rather than observation.

So the writer establishes at the outset that this is not a strange way to hold anything. His readers already order their whole understanding of reality around an event none of them saw — and he is about to ask them to keep ordering their lives around a promise they cannot see either.

There is a further thread here that runs through the chapter. If the visible came out of the invisible, then the invisible is the more solid of the two. That is the conviction Moses will act on when he endures “as seeing him who is invisible” (v.27), and the one these readers needed when their visible property was being carried out of their houses.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Abel offered to God a more acceptable sacrifice than Cain, through which he was commended as righteous, God commending him by accepting his gifts. And through his faith, though he died, he still speaks. By faith Enoch was taken up so that he should not see death, and he was not found, because God had taken him. Now before he was taken he was commended as having pleased God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“By faith Abel offered to God a more acceptable sacrifice than Cain.” Genesis does not say why Abel’s was accepted and his brother’s refused; it records the fact and moves on. The writer supplies the reason: faith.

Not the material of the offering, then, and not the technique. Two men brought what they had, and God saw what was underneath it. That is a sobering thing to know about worship, and it is the earliest instance in Scripture of the principle this letter keeps applying: the same act performed by two people is not the same act.

“Through his faith, though he died, he still speaks.” A beautiful sentence, and it works two ways. In Genesis it is Abel’s blood that cries out from the ground (Gen 4:10); here it is his faith that goes on speaking. He is the first man in the Bible to die and the first to be murdered, and he is still saying something to a congregation four thousand years later.

Notice this about the whole chapter. Everyone in it is dead, and every one of them is still talking.

“By faith Enoch was taken up so that he should not see death.” The shortest biography in Genesis: he walked with God, and he was not, for God took him (Gen 5:24). In a chapter of Genesis that records the years and the death of every generation, one man has no death recorded.

“Before he was taken he was commended as having pleased God.” The Greek Old Testament renders “walked with God” as “pleased God”, which is where the writer gets the phrase — and it supplies the hinge into verse 6.

Set the two men side by side and the chapter has already made an important point. Abel died young and violently; Enoch did not die at all. Faith produced opposite outcomes in the first two examples, and both are commended. Anyone reading this chapter as a list of what faith gets you has been warned in the first two verses of the gallery.

verseByVerse.quote: And without faith it is impossible to please him, for whoever would draw near to God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And without faith it is impossible to please him.”

The word is impossible again — the letter’s absolute, used of restoring apostates (6:4), of God lying (6:18), and of bulls and goats taking away sins (10:4). It is not that faithless obedience is inferior. It cannot please him at all.

That should be allowed to land, because it cuts against a very natural assumption. A person may live decently, give generously, and behave better than most of the congregation, and none of it registers as pleasing God if it is not done in faith. Paul says the same thing from the other side: whatever does not proceed from faith is sin (Rom 14:23).

The reason is not arbitrary. To do good without trusting God is to treat him as somebody to be managed rather than believed — and no relationship can be pleased by a partner who does not take the other at his word.

Then the two things anyone drawing near must believe, and they are strikingly modest.

“That he exists.” Not a developed doctrine of God. That he is there.

“And that he rewards those who seek him.” That he is worth approaching — that the seeking is not into an empty room.

Notice that the second is the harder of the two. A great many people believe God exists and behave as though seeking him were pointless; the practical atheism of the half-believing is not a denial of God’s existence but a settled expectation that nothing will come of approaching him. Hebrews says faith is precisely the confidence that something will.

And the reward-language should not be apologised for. It runs through the chapter — Moses was looking to the reward (v.26), the patriarchs to a city (v.10). Seeking God for what he gives is only mercenary if what he gives is something other than himself. It is not.

What about those who have never heard? This verse does not say that a vague belief in God is enough. The faith that pleases God draws near to him through Christ (7:25), and the God who rewards those who seek him is the God who sends them the message, as he sent Peter to Cornelius (Acts 10). Some Christians hold that God may save those who respond sincerely to what they know of him, or that he will give them a chance after death. But Scripture offers no such promise, and this letter closes the door on a second chance (9:27). Creation leaves everyone without excuse (Rom 1:20), but salvation comes by hearing the gospel (Rom 10:14). The answer is not to speculate about them but to go to them.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Noah, being warned by God concerning events as yet unseen, in reverent fear constructed an ark for the saving of his household. By this he condemned the world and became an heir of the righteousness that comes by faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“By faith Noah, being warned by God concerning events as yet unseen, in reverent fear constructed an ark.”

Everything in this verse turns on the phrase about the unseen. Noah was told about something for which there was no evidence whatever — and if the world before the flood was as Scripture suggests, quite possibly about rain he had never watched fall.

“In reverent fear” is one word meaning godly caution. It is the same disposition credited to Christ at 5:7. Noah took God seriously, which is the whole of his commendation.

“Constructed an ark.” And here is where faith becomes visible. It was not a private conviction; it was a very large wooden object in a field, taking decades, in full view of neighbours who had every reason to think him mad.

That is what this chapter means by faith throughout, and it should be stated plainly because the word has softened in modern use. Not one person in this gallery is commended for holding an opinion. Every single one is commended for something they did that made no sense apart from a word from God.

“For the saving of his household.” The obedience of one man carried seven other people through. It is the same pattern as Rahab in verse 31, and it should be noticed by anyone whose family is watching them believe.

“By this he condemned the world.” Not by preaching at it, though Peter calls him a herald of righteousness (2 Pet 2:5). By building. A man taking God at his word in public passes a verdict on everyone who has heard the same word and done nothing — not by criticising them but simply by acting as though it were true.

“And became an heir of the righteousness that comes by faith.” The phrase is Paul’s, and it is placed here on a man who lived before Abraham, before the law, before circumcision. The righteousness that comes by faith is not a New Testament invention. It is how it has always worked.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to go out to a place that he was to receive as an inheritance. And he went out, not knowing where he was going. By faith he went to live in the land of promise, as in a foreign land, living in tents with Isaac and Jacob, heirs with him of the same promise. For he was looking forward to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called… and he went out, not knowing where he was going.”

That last clause is one of the great descriptions of faith in Scripture, and the order of events is the point. He obeyed first and found out afterwards. God said go, and did not say where until he had gone.

Consider what it cost in that world. A man of seventy-five leaving his father’s household (Gen 12:1–4), having already left the city of Ur, for an unnamed destination, with no map, no contract, and no possibility of verifying anything he had been told. Security in that culture was land and kin, and he left both.

“By faith he went to live in the land of promise, as in a foreign land, living in tents.”

Here is the sharper irony, and the writer means it to be felt. He arrived, and he was still a stranger. The land was promised to him and he never owned a field in it — the only ground he ever bought was a cave to bury his wife in (Gen 23). He lived in a tent for a hundred years in the country God had given him.

“With Isaac and Jacob, heirs with him of the same promise.” Three generations under canvas. The son and the grandson inherited the promise and the tent together, and none of the three saw it kept.

“For he was looking forward to the city that has foundations.”

And there is the explanation, in the contrast between a tent and a city with foundations. A tent is the least permanent structure a man can live in — pegs and cloth, moved every season. Foundations are the opposite: the part of a building that does not move.

Abraham could live in the temporary because he was expecting the permanent. That is the logic of the whole chapter and it is the answer to the readers’ situation: people whose houses had been emptied, told about a man who never had a house and did not mind, because he was waiting for something with foundations.

“Whose designer and builder is God.” The words are an architect’s and a craftsman’s. Abraham never saw the city; he did know who was building it.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Sarah herself received power to conceive, even when she was past the age, since she considered him faithful who had promised. Therefore from one man, and him as good as dead, were born descendants as many as the stars of heaven and as many as the innumerable grains of sand by the seashore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“By faith Sarah herself received power to conceive, even when she was past the age.”

The commendation is generous, and any reader of Genesis will feel the generosity. Sarah laughed when she overheard the promise, and then denied laughing (Gen 18:12–15). She had earlier arranged a substitute in Hagar rather than wait. Her faith was not straightforward.

And Hebrews says: by faith. This is one of the clearest instances in Scripture of God commending what he sees underneath a mixed performance. He is not describing her as she behaved on her worst afternoon. He is describing what was actually there, and it was genuine.

“Since she considered him faithful who had promised.” There is the thing itself, and it is the same phrase as 10:23 — he who promised is faithful. Faith in this chapter is repeatedly a judgement about the character of the promiser rather than a feeling about the promise.

“Therefore from one man, and him as good as dead…” The phrase is blunt and Paul uses it too (Rom 4:19). A hundred-year-old body and a ninety-year-old womb, and the writer does not soften either.

That is important to the argument, because faith here is not optimism about the possible. Abraham and Sarah were not hoping for a favourable outcome within the range of nature. The situation was, humanly, closed — and the New Testament is careful to say so rather than pretend the odds were merely long.

“Were born descendants as many as the stars of heaven and as many as the innumerable grains of sand.” The two images are God’s own from the Genesis promises, and they were given to a childless man on a particular night, when he was taken outside and told to look up (Gen 15:5).

From one man as good as dead, a nation. And the readers of this letter were the proof — they were the sand, sitting in a room somewhere, hearing about the night their ancestor was told to count stars.

verseByVerse.quote: These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar, and having acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth. For people who speak thus make it clear that they are seeking a homeland. If they had been thinking of that land from which they had gone out, they would have had opportunity to return. But as it is, they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The writer pauses the roll-call to say what all of them had in common, and it is not what a modern reader expects from a chapter about faith.

“These all died in faith, not having received the things promised.”

They died without receiving what was promised, but they did not die without salvation. They were saved as we are, by faith in God’s promise of the Christ who was to come, and his death covers their sins too (9:15).

Read that against any account of faith that measures it by results. Every one of them died without getting it. Abraham never owned the land, never saw the nation, never met the offspring in whom all families would be blessed. He got Isaac and a burial cave.

“But having seen them and greeted them from afar.” The image is of travellers sighting a country from the deck of a ship and waving at a shore they will not reach on this voyage. They saw it. They were glad. They did not land.

“And having acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth.” That is Abraham’s own description of himself when he came to buy the burial cave: I am a sojourner and foreigner among you (Gen 23:4).

“For people who speak thus make it clear that they are seeking a homeland.” The writer listens to how they talked and draws a conclusion from it. A man who calls himself a stranger has told you he belongs somewhere else.

Then verse 15 closes the obvious escape: “If they had been thinking of that land from which they had gone out, they would have had opportunity to return.” Ur was still there. The road ran both ways, and nobody was stopping them. Their homesickness was not for anywhere they had left.

“But as it is, they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one.” The letter’s word again: better.

“Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God.” And that is one of the most moving sentences in Scripture. He calls himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob — three men who lived in tents and died holding nothing — and the writer says he is not embarrassed by the association. People who are visibly waiting for another country do not embarrass him. It is the ones who have settled here who make the title awkward.

“For he has prepared for them a city.” The reason he is not ashamed is that their hope is not a fantasy. He has actually built the thing.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac, and he who had received the promises was in the act of offering up his only son, of whom it was said, “Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.” He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead, from which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac.” Genesis 22, the hardest chapter in the Old Testament, and the writer takes it as the summit of Abraham’s faith rather than as a problem to be explained.

“He who had received the promises was in the act of offering up his only son… of whom it was said, Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.”

The writer sets out the contradiction deliberately, because it is the point. Everything God had promised depended on this boy. He was the promise, in a body. And God told Abraham to kill him.

So the test was not merely whether Abraham loved God more than his son, terrible as that is. It was whether he would obey a command that appeared to destroy the promise it came from. He was being asked to trust God against God.

How could God command a father to sacrifice his son? He never intended it to be carried out. It was a test (Gen 22:1), and God stopped Abraham’s hand: Do not lay your hand on the boy (Gen 22:12). The same God forbade child sacrifice in the plainest terms (Lev 18:21; Deut 12:31). The story is unique, and it points beyond itself: God spared Abraham’s son and did not spare his own Son (Rom 8:32). It gives no one warrant to harm anyone in God’s name.

“He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead.”

“Considered” is a reckoning word — he worked it out. This was not blind obedience or a suspension of thought. Abraham reasoned: the promise runs through Isaac; God does not lie; therefore if Isaac dies, God will raise him. It is arithmetic, and it is the only arithmetic that fits both facts.

And it is remarkable, because no one had ever been raised from the dead. There was no precedent in the world for what Abraham concluded God would do. He inferred the resurrection from the character of God alone.

Genesis records the conclusion in his own words, when he tells the servants to wait: “I and the boy will go over there and worship and come again to you” (Gen 22:5). He said we.

“From which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back.” The word is parabole — in a parable. Isaac was as good as dead and came back down the mountain alive, and the whole episode is a picture: a father, an only son, wood carried up a hill, and a substitute provided by God at the last moment. Abraham named the place “the LORD will provide”, and two thousand years later, on a hill in the same region, he did.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Isaac invoked future blessings on Jacob and Esau. By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph, bowing in worship over the head of his staff. By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the exodus of the Israelites and gave directions concerning his bones.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three men in three verses, and what unites them is easily missed: all three acts of faith are performed by dying men about a future they will not see.

“By faith Isaac invoked future blessings on Jacob and Esau.” Remember how that scene actually went. Isaac was blind, deceived by his wife and younger son, and intended the blessing for Esau. He was, in the plainest terms, taken in.

Yet when he discovers the deception, he trembles violently and then says of Jacob: “yes, and he shall be blessed” (Gen 27:33). That is the moment Hebrews commends. Isaac recognised that God’s purpose had gone through his own mistake, and he did not try to undo it.

“By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph.” Another old blind man, and another crossing of hands — Jacob deliberately gave the greater blessing to the younger, over Joseph’s objection (Gen 48:14–19). The man who had stolen a blessing by deceit gives one away, at the end, by the same principle he had once tried to force.

“Bowing in worship over the head of his staff.” The detail is tender. An old man too weak to stand unsupported, leaning on a staff, as he had once crossed the Jordan with nothing but a staff (Gen 32:10), worshipping.

“By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the exodus of the Israelites and gave directions concerning his bones.”

This is the most striking of the three. Joseph was the second man in Egypt, with a palace, a title and a family established in the best land of the country. Nothing in his circumstances suggested that his descendants would ever leave, and the exodus was centuries away.

And he made them swear to carry his coffin out when they went. He would not be embalmed into an Egyptian tomb, however grand. His faith took the form of a funeral instruction — a set of bones in a box, sitting in Egypt for centuries as a standing statement that this was not home.

They kept the promise. Moses took the bones (Exod 13:19), and they were buried at Shechem after the conquest (Josh 24:32). The box travelled forty years in the wilderness.
verseByVerse.note: “Over the head of his staff” follows the Greek Old Testament of Gen 47:31; the Hebrew text reads “bed.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–40 — The Turn: Some Were Tortured
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
By faith Moses was hidden three months by parents unafraid of the king’s edict (v.23); grown, he refused to be called Pharaoh’s daughter’s son (v.24), choosing mistreatment with God’s people over the fleeting pleasures of sin (v.25), counting the reproach of Christ greater wealth than Egypt’s treasures, looking to the reward (v.26). By faith he left Egypt unafraid, enduring as seeing him who is invisible (v.27), and kept the Passover and sprinkled the blood (v.28).

By faith the people crossed the Red Sea, while the Egyptians attempting it drowned (v.29); the walls of Jericho fell after seven days (v.30); and Rahab the prostitute did not perish, having welcomed the spies (v.31). Time would fail to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel and the prophets (v.32), who conquered kingdoms, stopped lions’ mouths (v.33), quenched fire, escaped the sword, were made strong out of weakness (v.34).

Women received back their dead — and some were tortured, refusing release, to rise to a better life (v.35); others suffered mocking, flogging, chains (v.36); they were stoned, sawn in two, killed with the sword, wandering in skins of sheep and goats, destitute and afflicted (v.37) — of whom the world was not worthy — in deserts and caves (v.38). And all these, commended through their faith, did not receive what was promised (v.39), since God had provided something better for us, that apart from us they should not be made perfect (v.40).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Chapter Turns Over Mid-Verse

In verse 35 faith that raised the dead becomes faith that was tortured to death — the same faith, opposite outcomes, both commended. Of such people the world was not worthy.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David and Samuel were far from consistent, and they are in the roll.

Now: All these died waiting for what the church now has; apart from us they are not made perfect.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that the child was beautiful, and they were not afraid of the king’s edict. By faith Moses, when he was grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin. He considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking to the reward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents.”

The first act of faith in the Moses section is not his. It belongs to a mother and father defying a royal edict with a baby in a basket. “They were not afraid of the king’s edict” — and Exodus tells us the midwives feared God rather than Pharaoh (Exod 1:17), which is the same calculation.

“By faith Moses, when he was grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter.”

Weigh what was refused. Whatever his exact standing, he was raised in the royal household of the greatest power on earth, with its education, wealth and prospects — Stephen says he was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians (Acts 7:22). He walked away from it at forty (Acts 7:23).

“Choosing rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin.”

The verb is a choosing word: he weighed two options and took one. And the two adjectives do all the work. The pleasures were real — the writer does not pretend Egypt was miserable — but fleeting, lasting a season. Set against them was mistreatment, which was also real, and permanent company: with the people of God.

That is the calculation this chapter keeps making, and it is not asceticism. It is arithmetic about duration.

“He considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt.” A startling phrase, since Moses lived some fourteen centuries earlier. It most likely means the reproach borne by God’s anointed people, and so by the Anointed One with whom they are identified — the same disgrace, in a different century.

“Greater wealth” is a deliberately commercial word, set against the literal treasures of the richest kingdom in the world. Moses did not weigh spiritual benefit against material loss. He weighed one wealth against another and concluded that reproach was the better asset.

“For he was looking to the reward.” The reason he could count that way, and it is verse 6 again. He was not being noble. He was looking at a figure the Egyptians could not see.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith he left Egypt, not being afraid of the anger of the king, for he endured as seeing him who is invisible. By faith he kept the Passover and sprinkled the blood, so that the Destroyer of the firstborn might not touch them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“By faith he left Egypt, not being afraid of the anger of the king.”

There is a difficulty here worth naming, since Exodus says Moses fled to Midian because he was afraid (Exod 2:14). The likeliest reading is that this refers to the exodus itself rather than the flight — the writer follows the order of events, and the Passover comes in the next verse. Others take it as describing the settled disposition of a life rather than one bad afternoon. Either way, Hebrews is not rewriting the history; it is characterising a man.

“For he endured as seeing him who is invisible.”

It is the finest sentence in the chapter, and the paradox is deliberate. Seeing the invisible — the writer puts two words together that cannot go together, in order to say what faith actually does.

And it connects back to verse 3. If the visible world was made out of what cannot be seen, then the invisible is the more solid of the two, and a man who reckons with it is not being fanciful but realistic. Moses stood in front of the most visible power on earth, unimpressed, because he was looking at somebody else in the room.

“Endured” is the word from 10:36 — remaining under weight. That is what the seeing produced: not a mystical experience but forty years of staying put.

“By faith he kept the Passover and sprinkled the blood.”

Consider what that instruction required. A lamb killed, and its blood painted on the doorposts of every Israelite house — and every firstborn son in the country would live or die that night on the strength of it. Nothing about blood on a doorframe would strike anyone as protective. Moses had only the word of God that it would work.

“So that the Destroyer of the firstborn might not touch them.” And the Israelites were not exempt by nationality. The angel passed over houses with blood on them, and only those — which is the letter’s whole argument in a single night’s history: not who you are descended from, but whether the blood has been applied.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith the people crossed the Red Sea as on dry land, but the Egyptians, when they attempted to do the same, were drowned. By faith the walls of Jericho fell down after they had been encircled for seven days. By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient, because she had given a friendly welcome to the spies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three acts of faith, and the writer has chosen them to make a point about who faith belongs to.

“By faith the people crossed the Red Sea as on dry land, but the Egyptians, when they attempted to do the same, were drowned.”

The same water, the same seabed, the same walls of water on either hand — and two entirely different outcomes. The Egyptians did precisely what Israel did and it killed them.

So the crossing was not a technique. What made the difference was not the action but what stood behind it, exactly as with Abel’s sacrifice in verse 4. This is the chapter’s consistent claim, and it carries into any consideration of religious practice: the same act performed by two people is not the same act.

“By faith the walls of Jericho fell down after they had been encircled for seven days.”

Here faith takes the form of doing something visibly absurd for a week. An army walking in silence round a fortified city, once a day, watched from the battlements by men who presumably found it very funny by the fourth morning. Nothing happened on days one through six.

That is a detail worth holding on to. Faith frequently looks foolish for a period before it looks like anything at all, and the seventh day is the only one anybody remembers.

“By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient.”

The writer keeps the description. He does not call her the innkeeper or pass over her history, and the placing is deliberate: immediately after Moses and the exodus stands a Canaanite woman of that trade, in the same list, commended on the same terms.

“Because she had given a friendly welcome to the spies.” She had heard what happened at the Red Sea and drew a conclusion the rest of her city refused: the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath (Josh 2:11). She had less evidence than anyone in Jericho and believed more.

But Rahab lied to the king’s men (Josh 2:4–5). Does Hebrews approve her lie? It commends her faith and her welcome of the spies, not every word she spoke. Christians differ on the lie itself. Some hold that deceiving those bent on murder is not the false witness the ninth commandment forbids, and point to the Hebrew midwives, with whom God dealt well (Exod 1:19–20). Others, with Augustine and Calvin, hold that the lie was a sin, forgiven like the rest of her past, and that God honoured her faith in spite of it. The second is the more likely, since Scripture never praises the lie itself. What it praises is a Canaanite woman who staked her life on Israel’s God.

Two things follow. She is one of only two women named in this chapter, and the only Canaanite — and she ended in the genealogy of Christ (Matt 1:5). If the readers of this letter were wondering whether the family of faith was narrowing, the answer is that it always had a Canaanite prostitute in it.

verseByVerse.quote: And what more shall I say? For time would fail me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, of David and Samuel and the prophets— who through faith conquered kingdoms, enforced justice, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the power of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, were made strong out of weakness, became mighty in war, put foreign armies to flight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And what more shall I say? For time would fail me…” The preacher looks at his material and gives up on the attempt to cover it — and the remark is a piece of skill, because the impression of an inexhaustible supply is stronger than another twenty examples would be.

Then six names, and they are not the ones we would have chosen. Gideon, who demanded two signs with a fleece. Barak, who would not go to battle unless a woman came with him. Samson, whose life was a catalogue of appetite and folly. Jephthah, who made a rash vow with terrible consequences. David, the adulterer and murderer. Samuel, whose sons took bribes.

Not one of them is a model of consistency, and the writer must have known it — his readers knew those stories far better than we do. He puts them in the roll of faith anyway, which tells you what the roll is measuring. Not achievement, and certainly not character. The bare fact of having taken God at his word, in the middle of lives that were often a mess.

Then nine achievements in two verses, rattled off at speed.

“Conquered kingdoms, enforced justice, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions” — Daniel. “Quenched the power of fire” — his three friends. “Escaped the edge of the sword” — David from Saul, Elijah from Jezebel.

Does obtained promises contradict v. 39? No. These men received particular promises in their lifetimes: victories, deliverances, sons. What none of them received was what was promised in the full sense, the coming of Christ and the city God has prepared.

“Were made strong out of weakness.” That one deserves its own moment, because it is the pattern of nearly every name on the list. Not strong men who stayed strong. Weak men who were made strong, which is a passive verb and locates the strength somewhere other than in them.

“Became mighty in war, put foreign armies to flight.” The list ends at its most triumphant — and the very next word in the chapter is “women received back their dead”, and then the whole thing turns over.
verseByVerse.note: Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah are from Judges; the lions’ mouths recall Daniel, and the fire recalls his three friends.

verseByVerse.quote: Women received back their dead by resurrection. Some were tortured, refusing to accept release, so that they might rise again to a better life. Others suffered mocking and flogging, and even chains and imprisonment. They were stoned, they were sawn in two, they were killed with the sword. They went about in skins of sheep and goats, destitute, afflicted, mistreated— of whom the world was not worthy—wandering about in deserts and mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The turn comes mid-verse, and it is the most important structural feature of the chapter.

“Women received back their dead by resurrection” — the widow of Zarephath, the Shunammite. Faith at its most spectacular: a dead child handed back alive.

“Some were tortured, refusing to accept release.”

And with that clause the chapter changes direction entirely. The word for tortured refers to being beaten to death on a rack or frame. “Refusing to accept release” means they were offered a way out and would not take it — the account in 2 Maccabees of the martyrs under Antiochus (2 Macc 6–7), which the readers probably knew, describes exactly that.

“So that they might rise again to a better life.” Same word as the first clause: resurrection. Some got their dead back by it; some died for it. The identical faith produced both.

Then the catalogue: “mocking and flogging, and even chains and imprisonment. They were stoned, they were sawn in two, they were killed with the sword.” Jewish tradition held that Isaiah was sawn in two under Manasseh; Zechariah was stoned in the temple court (2 Chr 24:21); Jeremiah was imprisoned in a cistern (Jer 38:6).

“They went about in skins of sheep and goats, destitute, afflicted, mistreated.” This is the prophet’s uniform — Elijah’s garment of hair (2 Kgs 1:8) — and it is a picture of the men God sent to Israel living like vagrants in the country they were sent to.

Then, in the middle of the squalor, the writer interrupts himself: “of whom the world was not worthy”.

It is the great reversal of the chapter and one of the finest asides in Scripture. The world looked at these people in their goatskins, sleeping in caves, and reckoned them worthless. God’s verdict is that the world was not good enough for them. The judgement ran the other way.

And this is the paragraph the letter’s readers most needed. A congregation whose property had been plundered could look at the first half of the list and wonder why their faith had produced no such deliverance. The second half says: it produced these people too, and God is not ashamed of them either.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish tradition says the prophet Isaiah was sawn in two under King Manasseh.

verseByVerse.quote: And all these, though commended through their faith, did not receive what was promised, since God had provided something better for us, that apart from us they should not be made perfect.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“And all these, though commended through their faith, did not receive what was promised.”

The chapter ends where verse 13 stood: with everybody still waiting. The conquerors and the sawn-in-two, the ones who shut lions’ mouths and the ones the lions ate — all commended, none satisfied.

“Since God had provided something better for us.” And there is the reason, and it is astonishing. They did not receive it because God had something better in view, and the something better involves us.

“That apart from us they should not be made perfect.”

Read that slowly. Abraham cannot be completed without the congregation that first heard this letter read. Moses waits on us. The whole company of the Old Testament faithful is not brought to its end separately and earlier, but together with people who were not born for centuries.

Where, then, were the Old Testament saints in the meantime? Some traditions teach that they waited in a holding place below until Christ descended to set them free. Scripture gives little ground for that. Jesus told the dying thief, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43), and this letter speaks of the spirits of the righteous made perfect already in God’s presence (12:23). Believers who died before Christ were with God in conscious blessing. What they wait for, with us, is the resurrection of the body, the perfection that will come to the whole church together.

What is the “something better”? Everything the letter has been arguing: the better covenant, the better sacrifice, the better priest. They lived on promises; we live after the fulfilment. They saw the shadow and greeted it from afar; we have the substance.

Which places the readers of this letter in a position they had entirely failed to appreciate. They were drifting back toward the era these giants had lived in and longed to escape — and the whole gallery of them had died waiting for what this discouraged little congregation actually possessed.

“Made perfect” is the letter’s word: brought to completion. And the final note is one of solidarity across the centuries. There is one people of God, not two. Everyone in this chapter and everyone reading it arrives at the same moment, by the same faith, through the same sacrifice — and the writer is about to say what that means for people who are tired: they are not running alone, and the stands are full.
